name: Classic-Style Test 1
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City planner: Some residents argue that Harlow’s downtown parking garage should be demolished because it is rarely more than half full. But the garage’s low usage reflects its high hourly rates, which the council set before the new transit line reduced downtown traffic. Lowering those rates would probably fill the garage. So the garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the city planner’s argument?
choices: The garage is rarely more than half full because its hourly rates are high.
The downtown garage should not be demolished before lower rates have been tried.
Lowering the garage’s hourly rates would probably fill the garage.
The council set the garage’s rates before the transit line reduced downtown traffic.
Residents who want the garage demolished have misjudged how heavily it is used.
questions.explanation: The planner’s point, signaled by “So,” is that the garage should be kept until lower rates are tried, which is (B). (C) is the tempting choice, but the prediction about lower rates is offered as a reason for keeping the garage, not as the claim being argued for; (A) is likewise a supporting premise. (E) misreads the planner, who accepts that usage is low and disputes only its cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Low usage is caused by high rates, set before the transit line cut traffic; lowering the rates would probably fill the garage.

breakdown.analysis: This is a rebuttal. The residents say tear it down because it's half empty. The planner says the emptiness comes from the prices, cheaper prices would fill it, so keep it until we try that. The word "So" flags the conclusion, and everything before it is support. Think of a restaurant owner saying: "The new dish isn't selling because it's overpriced, a lower price would sell it, so don't pull it off the menu yet." The point is "don't pull it yet," not the pricing story.

choices.note: This is a premise. The planner uses the high-rates explanation to undercut the residents' reason. It supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.

CORRECT. "Kept, at least until lower rates have been tried" means the same thing as "not demolished before lower rates have been tried." It's what the "So" introduces and what every other sentence is there to support.

This is the trap. It's the planner's boldest claim, so it feels like the point. But ask why the planner says it: to show the garage is worth keeping. A prediction offered as a reason is a premise. Lesson: the conclusion is the claim the others are trying to prove, not the most interesting one.
Background detail. It explains why the rates are now too high. It sits at the bottom of the support structure.
The planner never says the residents misjudged usage. The planner accepts that the garage is rarely more than half full and only disputes what that fact means. Wrong claim attributed to the speaker.

questions.stimulus: Pet columnist: In a survey of dog owners, those who walk their dogs on retractable leashes reported far more incidents of their dogs lunging at passersby than did those who use fixed-length leashes. Evidently, the extra slack that retractable leashes provide encourages dogs to lunge.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on reports from dog owners rather than on the judgments of professional trainers
presumes that any dog that lunges at passersby must have been poorly trained
takes for granted that every dog walked on a retractable leash lunges at passersby
overlooks the possibility that owners of dogs prone to lunging are more likely to choose retractable leashes
treats the fact that lunging is undesirable as evidence that it is common
questions.explanation: The columnist infers that the leash causes the lunging from a mere correlation, ignoring that the dogs themselves may differ: owners of excitable, lunge-prone dogs might favor retractable leashes, which is (D). (A) is tempting because self-reports can be unreliable, but nothing in the argument turns on the owners being worse judges than trainers of whether their dogs lunge. (C) attributes a claim about every dog that the columnist never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extra slack of retractable leashes encourages dogs to lunge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Owners using retractable leashes reported far more lunging incidents than owners using fixed-length leashes.

breakdown.analysis: Classic correlation-to-causation. Retractable leash and lunging go together, so the columnist says the leash causes the lunging. But the arrow could run the other way, or the groups could just be different dogs. Maybe owners of wild, pully dogs pick retractable leashes because the dogs hate short leads. It's like saying hospitals make people sick because people in hospitals are sicker than people outside. Prephrase: the argument ignores that the dogs on retractable leashes may already be more lunge-prone.

choices.note: Tempting, because self-reports can be shaky. But owners are perfectly able to notice their dog lunging, and nothing in the argument depends on owners being worse judges than trainers. This names a source problem the argument doesn't really have.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our customers say our coffee is the best in town, so it must be better than any coffee a professional taster has rated.

choices.note: Training never comes up. The columnist blames the leash, not poor training, so this describes an assumption the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of flaw: That dog jumped on a guest, so its owner obviously never trained it.

choices.note: Too strong. The columnist talks about more incidents in one group, not that every retractable-leash dog lunges. The argument doesn't need or assume an "every" claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Retractable leashes encourage lunging, so my neighbor's dog, which is on one, must lunge at people.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the alternative explanation: the dogs differ before the leash ever enters the picture. If lunge-prone dogs end up on retractable leashes, the leash type would correlate with lunging even if slack had zero effect.
The argument never says lunging is undesirable, and it's not trying to prove lunging is common. It's a causal claim about leashes. Describes a different flaw entirely.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Littering is terrible, so it must be happening all over this park.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant owner: Last spring we began printing calorie counts on our menu. Since then, sales of our two highest-calorie desserts have fallen by nearly a third, while sales of our fruit plates have risen. So the calorie counts led many of our customers to choose lighter desserts.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the restaurant owner’s argument?
choices: Over the same period, dessert sales at nearby restaurants that do not print calorie counts showed no comparable shift.
Several customers have told the owner that they appreciate seeing calorie counts on the menu.
The restaurant’s highest-calorie desserts are also among its most expensive desserts.
Many of the restaurant’s customers say they rarely read the menu closely before ordering.
Last spring the restaurant also hired a new pastry chef, who redesigned the fruit plates.
questions.explanation: The owner attributes a sales shift to the calorie counts, so the argument is helped by evidence that the shift did not happen where there were no calorie counts, as (A) shows; that makes a general change in tastes a less likely cause. (B) is tempting but shows only that customers like the counts, not that the counts changed what they ordered. (E) offers a rival explanation and (D) suggests customers ignored the counts, so both weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The calorie counts led many customers to choose lighter desserts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the menu started showing calorie counts, sales of the two highest-calorie desserts fell almost a third and fruit plate sales rose.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causal argument. Calorie counts went up, then heavy dessert sales went down, so the counts did it. The weak spot: something else could have changed at the same time, like a citywide diet trend or the season. To strengthen, rule out those rivals. The cleanest way is a control group: places without calorie counts that didn't see the shift. It's like testing a new fertilizer: your tomatoes grew bigger, but did your neighbor's unfertilized tomatoes grow bigger too?

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the control group. Nearby restaurants without calorie counts saw no similar shift, so a general change in tastes or the weather is less likely to be the cause. That leaves the calorie counts looking more like the reason.
Tempting, but liking the counts isn't the same as changing what you order. A customer can appreciate the information and still order the chocolate cake. Doesn't connect counts to choices.
If anything this hurts. If the heavy desserts are also the priciest, maybe people cut back because of price. It opens a rival cause rather than supporting the calorie explanation.
This weakens. If customers barely read the menu, it's hard for numbers printed on the menu to be driving their choices.

Weakens. A new pastry chef who redesigned the fruit plates is a rival explanation for why fruit plates got more popular, at exactly the same time. Lesson: an answer that adds a second change during the same period almost always hurts a before-and-after argument.

questions.stimulus: The Ridgeway Observatory replaced its telescope with a new one whose much larger mirror gathers far more light, making faint galaxies easier to detect. Yet in its first year of use, the new telescope detected fewer faint galaxies in total than the old telescope had detected in its last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Telescopes with larger mirrors are more expensive to build than those with smaller mirrors.
The old telescope had been in use at the observatory for several decades.
Faint galaxies are considerably harder to detect than bright ones.
The observatory’s astronomers had expected the new telescope to detect many more faint galaxies than the old one.
In its first year, the new telescope was often shut down for calibration and so observed for far fewer hours.
questions.explanation: A better instrument can still produce a smaller total if it is used much less, and (E) says the new telescope spent far less time observing, which resolves the puzzle. (D) merely restates the expectation that makes the result surprising, and (C) is true of both telescopes alike, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new telescope gathers far more light and makes faint galaxies easier to detect, but in its first year it detected fewer faint galaxies in total than the old one did in its last year.

breakdown.analysis: A better tool produced a smaller total. Totals depend on two things: how good the tool is and how much it gets used. So look for something that made the new telescope get used less, or look at fewer parts of the sky. It's like buying a faster car and still logging fewer miles this year because it sat in the shop for months. Prephrase: the new telescope wasn't observing as much.

choices.note: Cost has nothing to do with how many galaxies it detects once it's built. Irrelevant.
So the old telescope was old. That makes it even stranger that it beat the new one. Doesn't resolve anything.

True of both telescopes equally. A fact that applies to both sides can't explain a difference between them. Lesson: in a paradox about a comparison, you need a factor that differs between the two things.
This just restates why the result is surprising. Expectations don't explain why the expectations weren't met.

CORRECT. Fewer hours of observing means fewer chances to detect anything. Even a far better telescope can rack up a smaller total if it's shut down for calibration much of the year. Both facts in the paradox can now be true.

questions.stimulus: At Corwin Insurance, most employees who requested a standing desk last year received one. Of the employees who received standing desks, most reported less back pain at the end of the year than at the start. Among employees who requested a standing desk but did not receive one, reports of back pain were essentially unchanged over the year.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most Corwin employees reported less back pain at the end of last year than at the start.
Standing desks are the most effective means of reducing back pain among office workers.
Using a standing desk may have helped reduce back pain for some Corwin employees.
Corwin employees who did not request standing desks reported no change in back pain.
Employees who received standing desks used them for most of each workday.
questions.explanation: The comparison between requesters who did and did not get desks gives modest support to the hedged claim in (C) that the desks may have helped some employees. (A) is the tempting trap: the statements concern only employees who requested desks, and nothing indicates that they make up most of the company. (B) is far too strong, and (D) and (E) concern matters the statements never address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Most employees who requested a standing desk got one; 2) most of those who got one reported less back pain at year's end; 3) requesters who didn't get one reported essentially unchanged back pain.

breakdown.analysis: We have a rough comparison: among people who all wanted a desk, the ones who got desks mostly improved, and the ones who didn't stayed the same. That's some evidence the desks helped, not proof (placebo, other changes, etc.). So the right answer will be modest: "may have helped some." Watch for answers that blow up the group from "requesters" to "all employees."

choices.note: The trap. The facts only cover people who requested desks. We have no idea whether requesters are most of the company. If only 20 of 500 employees asked, "most employees" improving doesn't follow. Wrong group.
Way too strong. "Most effective means" requires comparing standing desks to every other treatment, and we compared them to nothing at all.

CORRECT. Hedged and well backed. Desk recipients mostly improved while similar people without desks didn't, so it's reasonable to say desks may have helped some employees. "May" and "some" keep it safe.
The statements say nothing about employees who never requested a desk. Their back pain could have gone anywhere. Unsupported.
We never learn how much anyone used their desk. Getting one doesn't mean standing at it most of the day. Unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Our school stopped assigning weekend homework this year in order to reduce student stress. Yet students’ average score on the annual stress survey is no lower this year than it was last year. So eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the principal’s argument?
choices: Nothing else at the school this year raised student stress enough to mask a reduction caused by the policy.
Students who no longer have weekend homework spend more time on extracurricular activities.
Reducing the amount of homework is the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.
Students’ average score on the stress survey was higher this year than it was last year.
Most students had been completing their weekend homework before the policy took effect.
questions.explanation: Unchanged survey scores show the policy failed only if nothing else pushed stress up at the same time; if some other change raised stress by as much as the policy lowered it, the flat scores would hide a real effect. That is (A). (C) is tempting but goes much further than needed: the argument concerns whether this policy worked, not whether homework reduction is the best method. (D) is not required, since unchanged scores are enough for the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The policy started this year; average stress survey scores are no lower than last year.

breakdown.analysis: The principal reads flat scores as "the policy did nothing." But flat scores could hide two forces canceling out: the policy lowers stress while something else raises it. Picture a diet that works, but you also stopped exercising, and the scale doesn't move. The diet still worked. For the principal's conclusion to hold, nothing else can have been pushing stress up enough to mask the drop. Negation test: if negating a choice wrecks the argument, it's required.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, something else did raise stress enough to hide a real reduction. Then flat scores tell you nothing about the policy, and the conclusion falls apart. Negation destroys the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Something else at the school this year raised student stress enough to mask a reduction caused by the policy.

choices.note: Negate it and nothing happens. Whether students moved to extracurriculars or not, the argument is about the stress scores. Irrelevant.
choices.negation: Students who no longer have weekend homework do not spend more time on extracurricular activities.

choices.note: Too strong. The principal only claims this policy didn't work, not anything about which method is best. Negate it (homework cuts aren't the best method) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Reducing the amount of homework is not the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.

choices.note: Not required. "No lower" already does the job. Negated, scores weren't higher (say, exactly the same), and the argument works just fine.
choices.negation: Students' average score on the stress survey was not higher this year than it was last year.

choices.note: Tempting, since if kids weren't doing the homework anyway, cutting it couldn't help. But that would actually support the principal's conclusion. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument; it gives another reason the policy might not have worked.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students had been completing their weekend homework before the policy took effect.

questions.stimulus:
Ana: The old mill on Fenwick Creek should be restored and opened as a museum. It is the town’s last surviving link to the industry on which the town was founded, and visitors would learn how our community grew.

Ben: The mill is certainly the most historically important building in town. But restoring it would cost far more than the town could ever raise. A plaque and a small exhibit at the library would preserve the mill’s story at a fraction of the cost.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Ana and Ben agree that
choices: the mill should be restored and opened as a museum
restoring the mill would cost more than the town could raise
a library exhibit is an adequate substitute for a museum
the history associated with the mill is worth preserving in some form
visitors would be more interested in a museum than in a library exhibit
questions.explanation: Ana wants a museum to keep the mill’s history alive, and Ben calls the mill historically important and proposes a cheaper way to preserve its story, so both value preserving that history, as (D) says. (A) is Ana’s view only, while (B) and (C) are Ben’s alone. Neither speaker compares visitor interest, so (E) is unsupported.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ana: Restore the mill as a museum; it's the town's last link to its founding industry and teaches visitors how the town grew.; Ben: The mill is the most historically important building, but restoring it costs far too much; a plaque and library exhibit would preserve its story cheaply.

breakdown.analysis: This is an agreement question. They disagree about the method (museum vs. plaque and exhibit) but both want the mill's story preserved. Ben's "preserve the mill's story at a fraction of the cost" shows he values preserving it; he just wants it done cheaper. For agreement, both speakers have to be committed to the answer, not just one.

choices.note: That's exactly what they disagree about. Ana says yes; Ben says it costs too much.
Ben's view only. Ana never addresses cost, so we can't say she agrees.
Ben's view only. Ana wants a full museum and never says a library exhibit would be enough.

CORRECT. Ana wants a museum to keep the history alive. Ben calls the mill historically important and proposes a plaque and exhibit to "preserve the mill's story." Both are committed to preserving that history somehow. "In some form" is what makes this work.
Neither speaker compares visitor interest in a museum versus an exhibit. Unsupported for both.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director: Customers who bought our Lumo vacuum with the extended warranty brought it in for repairs less often than customers who bought it without the warranty. The warranty includes a free yearly tune-up that other customers do not receive. So the tune-up must be reducing breakdowns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director’s argument?
choices: Customers without the extended warranty must pay the full cost of any repair.
During each yearly tune-up, technicians fix any malfunction they find, and such fixes are not recorded as repair visits.
Lumo vacuums break down less often than most competing vacuums do.
Most customers who bought the extended warranty brought their vacuums in for the yearly tune-up.
The extended warranty costs about one-fifth as much as the vacuum itself.
questions.explanation: The director treats fewer recorded repair visits as evidence of fewer breakdowns. (B) shows the comparison is skewed: warranty holders’ malfunctions are often fixed during tune-ups and never counted as repairs, so their lower repair count need not mean fewer breakdowns. (D) strengthens the argument by confirming that warranty holders actually got the tune-ups, and (A), if anything, strengthens it: customers who must pay for repairs would tend to bring vacuums in less often, yet they still had more repair visits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The free yearly tune-up must be reducing breakdowns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Warranty customers brought their vacuums in for repairs less often than non-warranty customers; only warranty customers get the yearly tune-up.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the switch: the evidence is about repair visits, but the conclusion is about breakdowns. Those aren't the same thing. If breakdowns get fixed some other way, repair visits can drop even when breakdowns don't. It's like saying a gym's members get sick less because they file fewer sick-day forms, when the gym's clinic quietly treats them on site. Prephrase: warranty holders' breakdowns are being handled without counting as repair visits.

choices.note: If anything this strengthens. Non-warranty customers have to pay for repairs, which should make them come in less, yet they still came in more. That makes their higher repair rate look like real breakdowns.

CORRECT. Malfunctions get fixed during the tune-up and aren't recorded as repair visits. So warranty holders could break down just as often; their breakdowns just show up as tune-ups. The lower repair count no longer shows fewer breakdowns.
Comparing Lumo to competitors doesn't touch the comparison between warranty and non-warranty Lumo owners. Irrelevant.
This strengthens. It confirms warranty customers actually got the tune-ups, which the argument needs.
Price of the warranty is irrelevant to whether the tune-up reduces breakdowns. You might wonder if pricey warranties attract careful owners, but this choice doesn't say that.

questions.stimulus: Manager: An employee’s request to work a flexible schedule should be granted whenever the employee’s duties do not require being present at fixed hours, provided that granting the request would not shift any work onto coworkers and the employee has met every deadline during the past six months.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Rina’s duties do not require fixed hours, and she has met every deadline this year. So her request for a flexible schedule should be granted, even though coworkers would have to cover her morning calls.
Tomas has met every deadline for six months, and his flexible schedule would not burden his coworkers. So his request should be granted, even though he must staff the front desk from nine to five.
Lena’s duties do not require fixed hours, and no work would shift to her coworkers. But she missed a deadline last month, so her request for a flexible schedule should be denied.

Omar’s request would shift no work to his coworkers, and his duties do not require fixed hours. So his request should be granted, since his supervisor considers him one of the department’s best performers.
Priya’s work can be done at any hour, she has not missed a deadline in over a year, and her team confirms that none of her tasks would fall to them. So her request should be granted.
questions.explanation: The principle says a request should be granted when all three conditions hold, and only (E) establishes all three: no fixed hours, no missed deadlines in the past six months, and no work shifted to coworkers. (C) is the attractive trap: Lena fails one condition, but the principle states only when requests should be granted, so it cannot justify denying hers. (A) and (B) each fail a condition outright, and (D) never establishes that Omar has met his deadlines.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If duties don't require fixed hours AND granting won't shift work to coworkers AND the employee met every deadline in the past six months → the request should be granted.

breakdown.analysis: Three conditions, all needed, and the rule only tells you when to grant. It says nothing about when to deny. So the right answer must show all three conditions and conclude "grant." Any answer that concludes "deny" can't be justified by this rule: failing a sufficient condition doesn't trigger the opposite result. Like "if it's sunny and warm, we'll go to the beach" doesn't tell you you'll stay home if it's cloudy.

choices.note: Fails the coworker condition: coworkers would have to cover her morning calls. With a condition missing, the principle can't justify granting.
Fails the fixed-hours condition: he has to staff the front desk nine to five. Can't justify granting.

The trap. Lena does miss a condition, so it feels like the rule says no. But the rule only says when to grant. Failing it doesn't mean deny. Lesson: a sufficient condition that isn't met tells you nothing.
Never says Omar met his deadlines. Being a "best performer" isn't the same as meeting every deadline. Missing condition.

CORRECT. Work can be done at any hour (no fixed hours), no missed deadline in over a year (covers the past six months), and no tasks fall to the team (no work shifted). All three conditions hold, so the principle says grant.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Every project paid for from the city’s parks budget must be approved by the neighborhood advisory board, and the board approves only projects that are open to the public. The proposed rooftop garden on City Hall would be reachable only through a secured employee entrance. Thus, the rooftop garden cannot be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the council member’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The advisory board has approved every project it has reviewed that is open to the public.
Some projects paid for from the parks budget are not open to the public.
No facility that is reachable only through a secured employee entrance is open to the public.
The rooftop garden would benefit city employees more than it would benefit other residents.
If a project is open to the public, it can be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.explanation: The chain is: parks funding requires board approval, and board approval requires being open to the public. The missing link connects “reachable only through a secured employee entrance” to “not open to the public,” and (C) supplies it, so the garden cannot get approval and therefore cannot get funding. (A) and (E) reverse the conditionals and say what is enough for approval or funding, which cannot show that the garden is barred. (B) conflicts with the stated rules.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rooftop garden cannot be paid for from the parks budget.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Parks funding → board approval; board approval → open to the public; the garden is reachable only through a secured employee entrance.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Parks-funded → board-approved → open to public. Contrapositive: not open to public → not board-approved → not parks-funded. To get the conclusion, we need the garden to be not open to the public. The premise only says it's reachable only through a secured employee entrance. Missing link: secured-employee-entrance-only → not open to public. Plug that in and the chain runs all the way to "can't be paid for from parks."

choices.note: Reversed. This says open to public → approved, which is the sufficient direction for getting approval. We need something that blocks approval, not something that grants it.
This contradicts the rules: every parks project needs approval and approval needs public access, so no parks project can be closed to the public. And it doesn't link the garden to anything.
CORRECT. Secured-employee-entrance-only → not open to public. The garden is secured-entrance-only, so not open, so not approved, so not parks-funded. The conclusion follows with certainty.
Who benefits is irrelevant to the conditional rules. Doesn't link the garden to public access.
Reversed. Open to public → can be funded. That tells you what's enough to qualify, not what disqualifies. Doesn't get you to "cannot."

questions.stimulus: Science writer: Ten years ago, amateur astronomers discovered about 30 percent of all newly identified asteroids; last year, they discovered under 5 percent. Clearly, amateurs are finding fewer asteroids than they once did, perhaps because light pollution has worsened in the suburbs where many of them live.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the science writer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on figures drawn from only two years
overlooks the possibility that the total number of asteroids discovered each year has risen sharply
presumes without justification that light pollution affects professional astronomers less than it affects amateurs
takes for granted that most amateur astronomers live in suburbs
confuses a decline in amateurs’ interest in asteroids with a decline in their skill
questions.explanation: A falling share of discoveries does not show a falling number: if total discoveries grew enough, for example because professional survey telescopes came online, amateurs could be finding as many asteroids as before or more. (B) identifies this. (A) is tempting, but the argument’s problem is not too few data points; even many years of shrinking percentages would leave the same gap. (D) misstates the writer, who says only that “many” amateurs live in suburbs, and the light-pollution remark is offered only as a possible explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Amateurs are finding fewer asteroids than they once did (perhaps because of worse light pollution).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ten years ago amateurs found about 30% of newly identified asteroids; last year they found under 5%.

breakdown.analysis: Percent versus number. The evidence is about amateurs' share of discoveries; the conclusion is about how many they find. A share can shrink while the count stays flat or grows, if the total pie gets much bigger. Imagine amateurs found 30 of 100 asteroids then, and 40 of 1,000 now. Their share dropped from 30% to 4%, but they found more. Lesson: never jump from a percentage to an absolute number without knowing the total.

choices.note: Tempting, because two data points can be thin. But that isn't the real problem: even with ten years of steadily shrinking percentages, you'd still have the share-versus-number gap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: It rained on my birthday this year and last year, so it always rains on my birthday.

choices.note: CORRECT. If total discoveries exploded, say because professional survey telescopes came online, amateurs' share could plunge while their actual count held steady or rose. That's exactly the gap between "under 5 percent" and "fewer asteroids."
The writer doesn't compare how light pollution affects pros versus amateurs. The light-pollution bit is offered only as a "perhaps" explanation, and the main flaw is upstream of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smog hurts city runners' times, so it must be why city runners lose to suburban runners, even though we don't know smog affects suburban runners any less.

choices.note: Misreads the writer, who said "many" amateurs live in suburbs, not most. And nothing in the argument hinges on that.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Traffic is bad downtown, so most of our employees must have long commutes, since they surely all live downtown.

choices.note: Interest versus skill never comes up. The writer offers light pollution, not lost interest or lost skill, as a cause.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fewer kids are signing up for piano, so kids today must be worse at music.

questions.stimulus: At the Linden animal shelter, cats housed in the shelter’s quiet rooms have long been adopted more quickly than cats housed in the noisy main kennel area. Last fall, the shelter soundproofed another room and moved half of its main-area cats into it. Yet the cats that were moved were not adopted any more quickly than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why moving the cats did not shorten their adoption times?
choices: Cats in the main kennel area are frequently exposed to the noise of barking dogs.
Most people who adopt cats from the shelter visit on weekends.
The newly soundproofed room is larger than the shelter’s other quiet rooms.
Some cats in the main kennel area have been adopted within a day of arriving.
Until last fall, the shelter placed only its calmest and most sociable cats in quiet rooms.
questions.explanation: If the shelter had been putting its calmest, most sociable cats in the quiet rooms, those cats’ faster adoptions reflected their temperaments rather than the quiet, so giving other cats a quiet room would not be expected to help. That is (E). (A) is tempting because it explains why the main area might seem unappealing, but it gives no reason why removing the noise failed to help. (C) would, if anything, lead one to expect better results.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cats in the quiet rooms have long been adopted faster than cats in the noisy main area, but cats moved into a newly soundproofed room were adopted no faster than before.

breakdown.analysis: The shelter assumed the quiet caused the faster adoptions. If moving cats into quiet didn't help, maybe quiet was never the cause. Look for something else that made quiet-room cats special. It's like noticing that students in the honors classroom score higher, moving regular students into that room, and seeing no change: the room wasn't what made the honors students score higher. Prephrase: the quiet-room cats were different cats to begin with.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains why the main area is unpleasant. But that makes the puzzle worse: if noise is the problem, removing it should have helped. Doesn't explain the failure.
Weekend visiting applies to all cats equally. It doesn't explain why moved cats got no boost.
A bigger quiet room should, if anything, help more. This deepens the puzzle instead of solving it.
A few speedy main-area adoptions don't explain why the moved cats saw no improvement. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. The quiet rooms held the calmest, friendliest cats, and those traits are what got them adopted fast. The quiet itself wasn't doing the work. So moving ordinary cats into quiet wouldn't speed things up.

questions.stimulus: Food critic: A restaurant’s reputation for freshness depends on its use of ingredients that are in season. But a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients must change that menu several times a year, and frequent menu changes make it hard for a kitchen to prepare dishes consistently. Moreover, diners seldom return to a restaurant whose dishes are inconsistent. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients risks losing repeat customers
no restaurant can have both a reputation for freshness and a loyal base of repeat customers
restaurants that want repeat customers should avoid using seasonal ingredients
a reputation for freshness is less valuable to a restaurant than consistency is
restaurants whose dishes are consistent seldom use seasonal ingredients
questions.explanation: The premises connect an all-seasonal menu to frequent changes, frequent changes to difficulty with consistency, and inconsistency to diners not returning, so the cautious conclusion in (A) follows. (B) is the attractive overreach: the critic says only that consistency is hard, not impossible, and a restaurant could use seasonal ingredients without building its whole menu around them. (C) and (D) add recommendations or rankings the premises do not support, and (E) reverses the direction of the reasoning.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) A freshness reputation depends on using in-season ingredients; 2) an all-seasonal menu must change several times a year; 3) frequent menu changes make consistency hard; 4) diners seldom return to restaurants with inconsistent dishes.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the chain: all-seasonal menu → frequent changes → consistency is hard → (if inconsistent) diners seldom return. Notice the soft spot: "hard," not "impossible." So the honest ending is a risk, not a certainty. Prephrase: a restaurant with an all-seasonal menu risks losing repeat customers. Lesson: match the strength of the conclusion to the strength of the premises.

choices.note: CORRECT. It follows the chain and keeps the right strength. All-seasonal menus make consistency hard, and inconsistency drives diners away, so such restaurants risk losing repeat customers.
Overreach. "Hard" isn't "impossible," and a restaurant can lean on seasonal ingredients without building its entire menu around them. "No restaurant can" is far too strong.
A recommendation the premises don't support. The problem is building the menu entirely around seasonal ingredients, not using any at all.
Ranks freshness against consistency. The critic never says which is worth more.
Reverses the direction. The premises go from seasonal to inconsistent, not from consistent back to seasonal. Plenty of consistent restaurants could use seasonal ingredients in part of the menu.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Most of the buildings on Market Street date from before 1900, and most buildings in the city that date from before 1900 have been designated as landmarks. So most of the buildings on Market Street have been designated as landmarks.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Most members of the choir are sopranos, and most of the choir’s sopranos also play an instrument. So some members of the choir play an instrument.
Most of the library’s patrons are students, and all students receive free borrowing privileges. So most of the library’s patrons receive free borrowing privileges.
No member of the hiking club smokes, and most members of the hiking club are runners. So most runners do not smoke.
Most of the paintings in the east gallery are oil paintings, and most of the museum’s oil paintings are on loan. So most of the paintings in the east gallery are on loan.
Most of the apples grown on the Garza farm are sold at market. So most of the produce grown on the Garza farm is sold at market.
questions.explanation: The historian chains two “most” statements as if they guaranteed overlap: the Market Street buildings could fall mostly among the pre-1900 buildings that are not landmarks. (D) makes exactly that move with paintings, oil paintings, and loans. (A) is the strongest trap because it shares the “most… most” form, but its conclusion is only “some,” which does validly follow; (B) is also valid because its second premise says “all.” (C) and (E) are flawed, but in different ways, by reversing a relationship and by moving from a part to the whole.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Market Street buildings have been designated as landmarks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most Market Street buildings date from before 1900; most pre-1900 buildings in the city are landmarks.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Two "most" statements don't chain. Market Street's old buildings could be a small slice of the city's old buildings, and that slice could sit entirely in the non-landmark minority. Imagine 1,000 pre-1900 buildings citywide, 600 are landmarks, and Market Street's 50 old buildings are all among the 400 that aren't. Find the answer with the same most-most-so-most structure and the same flaw.

choices.note: The strongest trap: same "most... most" setup. But the conclusion is only "some," and that one is valid. Most choir members are sopranos, and most of those sopranos play an instrument, so at least some choir members play. Valid reasoning isn't a match for a flawed one.
Valid. "All students" get free borrowing, so whatever students are among the patrons get it, and that's most patrons. The "all" fixes the gap. Not a match.
Flawed, but differently. It flips the relationship: from "most hikers are runners" to a claim about most runners. Wrong flaw.

CORRECT. Most east gallery paintings are oils; most of the museum's oils are on loan; so most east gallery paintings are on loan. Same most-most-most chain, same flaw: the east gallery's oils could all be in the not-on-loan group.
Flawed, but it's a part-to-whole jump: apples are just one part of the farm's produce. Only one premise, no "most... most" chain. Wrong flaw.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Brightline advertises that its LED bulbs last 20 years, a figure based on tests of bulbs in open fixtures at room temperature. But heat shortens the life of LED bulbs, and most household light fixtures are enclosed, trapping heat around the bulb. So in most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the consumer advocate’s argument depends?
choices: Brightline’s competitors base their lifespan claims on more realistic tests.
Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is the main cause of LED bulb failure in households.
Brightline bulbs are not designed in a way that protects them from the effects of heat in enclosed fixtures.
Bulbs in enclosed fixtures fail sooner than bulbs in any other kind of fixture.
Brightline knowingly exaggerated the expected lifespan of its bulbs.
questions.explanation: The advocate moves from a general fact, that heat shortens LED life, to a prediction about Brightline bulbs in particular. If Brightline bulbs were built to withstand the heat of enclosed fixtures, that prediction would fail, so the argument requires (C). (B) is tempting but too strong: heat need only shorten these bulbs’ lives significantly, not be the leading cause of failure. (D) and (E) are likewise stronger than anything the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: In most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 20-year claim comes from tests in open fixtures at room temperature; heat shortens LED life; most household fixtures are enclosed and trap heat.

breakdown.analysis: The advocate goes from a general fact (heat shortens LED life) to a specific prediction about Brightline bulbs. That works only if Brightline bulbs are like typical LEDs in this respect. If Brightline built in a heat sink or some special design that shrugs off enclosed-fixture heat, the prediction fails. It's like saying "sun fades fabric, so this awning will fade" without checking whether it's UV-treated. Use the negation test on each choice.

choices.note: Negate it: competitors' tests are just as unrealistic. The argument about Brightline is unaffected. Not required.
choices.negation: Brightline's competitors do not base their lifespan claims on more realistic tests.

choices.note: Too strong. Heat only needs to shorten Brightline bulbs' lives a lot, not be the number one cause of failure. Negated, something else is the main cause, but heat could still cut lifespans well short of 20 years. Argument survives.
choices.negation: Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is not the main cause of LED bulb failure in households.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, Brightline bulbs are designed to resist enclosed-fixture heat. Then the general fact about heat wouldn't apply to them, and the prediction collapses. Negation wrecks the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Brightline bulbs are designed in a way that protects them from the effects of heat in enclosed fixtures.

choices.note: Too strong. Enclosed fixtures don't have to be the worst kind, just hot enough to shorten life. Negated, some other fixture is even worse, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Bulbs in enclosed fixtures do not fail sooner than bulbs in every other kind of fixture.

choices.note: Intent doesn't matter. The argument is about how long the bulbs last, not whether Brightline lied on purpose. Negated, an honest mistake, and the conclusion stands.
choices.negation: Brightline did not knowingly exaggerate the expected lifespan of its bulbs.

questions.stimulus: Superintendent: Critics claim that moving our high school’s start time from 7:30 to 8:30 has hurt attendance at after-school sports, because practices now end after dark. But this complaint is unfounded. The number of students on our sports teams this year is actually slightly higher than it was last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the superintendent’s defense?
choices: Attendance at the school’s evening theater and music rehearsals has also declined since the start time changed.
Unlike in previous years, students this year may remain on a team’s roster without attending a minimum number of practices.
Practices at neighboring schools that kept a 7:30 start time also end after dark during part of the year.
Membership on the school’s sports teams rose more this year than in any of the previous five years.
Several parents have complained that the later start time conflicts with their work schedules.
questions.explanation: The critics’ complaint is about attendance at practices, but the superintendent answers with roster size. (B) shows why that answer misses: with attendance no longer required to stay on a roster, rosters can grow even while practice attendance falls. (A) is the attractive trap, since it fits the critics’ general worry, but it concerns different activities and leaves the superintendent’s evidence about sports untouched. (D) supports the defense, and (C) and (E) do not bear on whether sports attendance fell.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics' complaint that the later start time hurt after-school sports attendance is unfounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The number of students on sports teams is slightly higher this year than last.

breakdown.analysis: The critics are talking about attendance at practice. The superintendent answers with roster size. Those are different things: you can be on a team and skip practice. Like a gym bragging about membership numbers when the complaint was that nobody shows up anymore. To weaken, show that roster size can rise while attendance falls.

choices.note: The trap. It fits the critics' general worry, but it's about theater and music, not sports. The superintendent's evidence about sports is untouched.

CORRECT. This year, students can stay on a roster without attending a minimum number of practices. So rosters can grow even as kids skip dark practices. The superintendent's numbers no longer answer the complaint.
Neighboring schools' practices also end after dark sometimes. That doesn't say anything about whether attendance at this school fell. Irrelevant.
Strengthens the superintendent: membership rose even more than usual. It doesn't expose the membership-versus-attendance gap.
Parents' work schedules are a different complaint. Nothing here about sports attendance.

questions.stimulus: Pelham city ordinance: A food truck may operate downtown only if it holds a downtown permit. A downtown permit is issued only to trucks that have passed the city’s fire inspection. A truck that uses a propane grill passes the fire inspection only if the grill has an automatic shutoff valve.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any food truck that has passed the city’s fire inspection may operate downtown.
Every food truck whose propane grill has an automatic shutoff valve passes the fire inspection.
A food truck that does not use a propane grill can be issued a downtown permit if it applies for one.
Some food trucks that operate downtown use propane grills.
A truck that has only ever used a propane grill lacking an automatic shutoff valve cannot be issued a downtown permit.
questions.explanation: A permit requires passing inspection, and a truck with a propane grill passes only if the grill has a shutoff valve; a truck whose propane grill has never had one could never have passed, so it cannot get a permit, as (E) says. (A) and (B) treat necessary conditions as if they were sufficient, (C) assumes that lacking a propane grill guarantees a permit, and (D) asserts the existence of trucks that the rules never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Operate downtown → downtown permit; 2) downtown permit → passed fire inspection; 3) propane-grill truck passes inspection → grill has automatic shutoff valve.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: operate downtown → permit → passed inspection. For propane trucks, passed inspection → shutoff valve. Contrapositive: propane grill with no shutoff valve → can't pass inspection → no permit → can't operate downtown. All these are necessary conditions. Meeting one doesn't guarantee the next step up. Lesson: "only if" introduces what's required, not what's enough.

choices.note: Reverses the chain. Passing inspection is required for a permit, and a permit is required to operate, but nothing says passing inspection is enough. You still need the permit.
Reverses the last rule. Having a shutoff valve is required to pass, not enough to pass. The truck could fail for some other reason.
Assumes that not using propane is enough to get a permit. The rules never say what guarantees a permit. The truck might still fail inspection.
Existence claim the rules never support. Conditional rules don't tell you any truck actually operates downtown or what grill it uses.
CORRECT. A truck whose only grill has always been a propane grill without a shutoff valve could never have passed inspection. No pass, no permit. This follows straight from the contrapositive chain.

questions.stimulus: Animal behaviorist: Parrots that pluck out their own feathers are commonly assumed to be bored. But feather plucking often begins in parrots that already have plenty of toys and companionship, and it frequently stops after a change in the bird’s diet. This suggests that, in many cases, plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause. Owners of parrots that pluck should therefore consult an avian veterinarian before buying more toys.
questions.stem: The claim that in many cases plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause plays which one of the following roles in the animal behaviorist’s argument?
choices: It is a conclusion drawn from evidence in the argument and is offered in support of the argument’s main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is a view that the argument is designed to call into question.
It is a premise offered in support of the view that plucking is usually caused by boredom.
It is a hypothesis offered to explain why parrot owners tend to buy more toys.
questions.explanation: The claim is drawn from the observations about toys and diet (“This suggests that”), and it in turn supports the recommendation introduced by “therefore,” so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (A) says. (B) is the trap: the argument’s final point is the advice to owners, which the nutritional claim supports. (C) describes the boredom assumption, not this claim, and (D) has the claim supporting the very view it opposes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Owners of plucking parrots should consult an avian vet before buying more toys.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plucking often starts in parrots with plenty of toys and company, and often stops after a diet change; so in many cases plucking has a nutritional, not psychological, cause.

breakdown.analysis: Three layers. Bottom: observations about toys and diet. Middle: "This suggests" plucking is often nutritional. Top: "therefore" owners should see a vet before buying toys. The claim in question is the middle layer: it's concluded from the evidence and then used to support the final advice. That's an intermediate (sub-) conclusion. Lesson: "therefore" after a supported claim usually means the earlier claim is a stepping stone.

choices.note: CORRECT. It's supported by the toys-and-diet observations ("This suggests") and in turn supports the recommendation introduced by "therefore." That's exactly an intermediate conclusion.
The trap. It's a conclusion, but not the main one. The final point is the advice to owners, and the nutritional claim is a reason for that advice.
The view the argument questions is the boredom assumption. This claim is the argument's own position, not its target.
Backwards. The claim opposes the boredom view; it doesn't support it.
The argument never tries to explain why owners buy toys. The claim explains plucking, not shopping habits.

questions.stimulus: Office manager: Only employees who have registered a vehicle with security may receive a parking pass, and security registers a vehicle only for an employee who has completed the safety orientation. Thus, Dana, who works only on weekends, will not receive a parking pass.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the office manager’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every employee who has completed the safety orientation will receive a parking pass.
The safety orientation is held only on weekdays.
Most employees who work only on weekends have not completed the safety orientation.
No employee who works only on weekends has completed the safety orientation.
Employees who work only on weekends rarely drive to work.
questions.explanation: A pass requires a registered vehicle, and registration requires completing the orientation. If no weekend-only employee has completed it, as (D) states, Dana cannot have a registered vehicle and so cannot receive a pass. (B) is the tempting choice, but an orientation held on weekdays could still have been attended by Dana, perhaps before she switched to weekends, so it does not guarantee the conclusion. (C) says only “most,” which leaves open that Dana completed it, and (A) reverses the conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dana, who works only on weekends, will not receive a parking pass.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Parking pass → registered vehicle; registered vehicle → completed safety orientation.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: pass → registered → completed orientation. Contrapositive: no orientation → no registration → no pass. To conclude Dana gets no pass, we need Dana to have not completed the orientation. The only thing we know about Dana is that she works only on weekends. Missing link: weekend-only → no orientation completed. It has to be airtight for Dana, so "most" won't do; we need "no weekend-only employee."

choices.note: Reversed. Orientation → pass gives a way to get a pass. We need a way to rule one out.

The tempting one. It feels like weekend workers couldn't attend a weekday session. But Dana might have done it on a weekday before switching to weekends, or come in specially. Doesn't guarantee she skipped it.
"Most" leaves room for Dana to be in the minority who did complete it. Sufficient assumptions need to guarantee the result, so "most" falls short.
CORRECT. Weekend-only → no orientation. Dana is weekend-only, so no orientation, so no registered vehicle, so no pass. The conclusion follows for sure.
"Rarely drive" doesn't link to the orientation rule at all, and "rarely" isn't "never." Dana might drive and still qualify.

questions.stimulus: Local historian: The diary of Hester Vane, who lived in Millbrook in the 1840s, describes crossing a covered bridge over the Tull River. Yet no other surviving record from that decade mentions such a bridge in Millbrook, and the town’s earliest map, drawn in 1852, shows no bridge over the Tull. So the bridge Vane described must have been in some other town along the river.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the local historian’s argument?
choices: Is Vane’s diary the oldest surviving document written by a Millbrook resident?
Were covered bridges more expensive to build in the 1840s than uncovered bridges?
Did some event destroy structures along the Tull River in Millbrook between the 1840s and 1852?
How long did Vane continue to live in Millbrook after the 1840s?
Were most residents of Millbrook in the 1840s able to read and write?
questions.explanation: The historian relies on the bridge’s absence from later evidence, especially the 1852 map. If a flood or similar event had destroyed a bridge in Millbrook before 1852, the map’s silence would be expected even though the bridge had existed, so the answer to (C) bears directly on the argument. (A) sounds important, but whether the diary is the oldest document does not affect whether the bridge was in Millbrook. The other questions do not bear on where the bridge stood.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The covered bridge Vane described must have been in some other town along the river, not Millbrook.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No other surviving 1840s record mentions a covered bridge in Millbrook; the town's earliest map (1852) shows no bridge over the Tull.

breakdown.analysis: The historian argues from absence: no record, no bridge on the 1852 map, so no bridge in the 1840s. The gap is time. A bridge could have existed in the 1840s and been gone by 1852. A good evaluate question is one where one answer helps the argument and the other hurts it. Ask: was there something that could have wiped the bridge out before 1852? Yes → the map's silence means little. No → the map is strong evidence.

choices.note: Sounds important but doesn't matter. Whether the diary is the oldest document says nothing about where the bridge stood. Either answer leaves the argument the same.
Cost of covered bridges doesn't tell us whether Millbrook had one. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If a flood or fire destroyed structures along the Tull in Millbrook before 1852, the map's missing bridge is expected even if Vane crossed one there; the argument weakens. If nothing like that happened, the map's silence is stronger evidence. Either answer moves the argument.
How long Vane stayed afterward doesn't tell us where the bridge was in the 1840s.
Literacy rates might explain why there are few records, but that's a stretch, and it says nothing about the 1852 map. Doesn't bear on where the bridge stood.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant reviewer: Café Morrow’s menu used to state that its bread was baked in-house. When the café began buying its bread from a local bakery, it simply removed that statement. Some diners complain that the café should have announced the change. But the café never made a false claim; it merely stopped making a true claim once the claim became false. So the café did nothing wrong.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the restaurant reviewer’s argument?
choices: Diners are entitled to be told the source of every ingredient in the food a restaurant serves them.
A business does nothing wrong in changing its suppliers so long as the quality of its products is unaffected.
A business that has made a false claim about its products should correct that claim promptly and publicly.
Whether a business has wronged its customers depends entirely on whether any of those customers was actually harmed.
A business that withdraws a claim about its products as soon as the claim becomes false need not announce the withdrawal.
questions.explanation: The reviewer’s defense is that the café stopped making the in-house claim at the moment it became false and so owed diners no announcement; (E) states exactly that principle. (B) is the strongest trap, but the reviewer says nothing about bread quality, and the diners’ complaint concerns the lack of an announcement, not the change of supplier. (C) is on topic but applies only to false claims, which the café never made, and (D) depends on harm, which the argument never discusses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Café Morrow did nothing wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The café never made a false claim; it simply stopped making the in-house-bread claim once that claim became false, without announcing the change.

breakdown.analysis: Diners say: you should have told us. The reviewer says: we dropped the claim the moment it stopped being true, so no announcement was owed. To justify that, we need a principle saying something like: if you withdraw a claim as soon as it becomes false, you don't have to announce the withdrawal. Lesson: a principle-justify answer has to connect the specific facts (quietly dropped a claim right when it became false) to the specific conclusion (did nothing wrong).

choices.note: Opposite direction. If diners are owed the source of every ingredient, the café arguably did wrong by not saying where its bread now comes from. This hurts the reviewer.

The strongest trap. It defends changing suppliers, but the diners aren't upset about the switch itself; they're upset there was no announcement. And the reviewer never mentions bread quality, so we can't even apply it.
On topic but doesn't apply: it's about false claims, and the café never made one. A rule for false claims can't tell us anything about a café that only ever made true ones.
Hinges on harm, which the reviewer never discusses. We don't know if any diner was harmed, so we can't apply it to reach "did nothing wrong."

CORRECT. The café withdrew the in-house claim exactly when it became false. This principle says such a business need not announce the withdrawal. That's precisely the diners' complaint answered, so the café did nothing wrong.

questions.stimulus: Councilor Reyes: Supporters of the proposed bus-only lane on Garnet Avenue claim that it will cut commute times for bus riders, because a similar lane in Easton did so. But buses in Easton run twice as often as ours do, so Easton’s results tell us little about what would happen on Garnet Avenue. Hence, the bus lane will not cut commute times for our riders.
questions.stem: The argument’s reasoning is questionable in that the argument
choices: relies on an analogy between two cities that differ in a relevant respect
takes the inadequacy of the evidence offered for a claim as showing that the claim is false
attacks the motives of the lane’s supporters rather than the reasoning they offer
presumes that bus frequency is the only factor that affects bus riders’ commute times
overlooks the possibility that the bus lane would benefit people who drive private cars
questions.explanation: Reyes legitimately shows that the Easton comparison is weak support, but then concludes that the lane will not cut commute times; a poorly supported claim may still be true, so (B) names the flaw. (A) is the main trap: the weak analogy belongs to the supporters, and pointing it out is the sound part of Reyes’s reasoning. (D) also tempts, but Reyes treats frequency only as one relevant difference, not as the sole factor, and (E) concerns drivers rather than bus riders.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bus lane will not cut commute times for Garnet Avenue riders.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Supporters cite Easton's bus lane; but Easton's buses run twice as often, so Easton's results tell us little about Garnet Avenue.

breakdown.analysis: Reyes does something fair, then something unfair. Fair: Easton is a weak comparison, so the supporters' evidence is weak. Unfair: concluding that the lane won't work. Weak evidence for a claim isn't evidence against it. It's like saying "Your only reason for thinking it'll rain is that your knee hurts, which is silly, so it won't rain." It still might. Lesson: knocking down an argument doesn't prove the opposite.

choices.note: The main trap. There is a shaky analogy here, but it belongs to the supporters. Reyes points it out, which is the sound part of the argument. Reyes isn't the one relying on it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Rome's new subway was a huge success, so our town of 5,000 should build a subway too.

choices.note: CORRECT. Reyes shows the Easton evidence is weak, then concludes the lane will not cut commute times. A poorly supported claim can still be true. Showing the evidence is bad doesn't show the claim is false.
Reyes never says anything about why supporters want the lane. The attack is on their evidence, not their motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The developer says the new mall will help the town, but he'd make millions from it, so his argument is worthless.

choices.note: Tempting, but Reyes treats bus frequency as one relevant difference that undermines the comparison, not as the only thing that matters for commute times.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our buses run as often as Easton's, so our commute times must be just like theirs.

choices.note: The argument is about bus riders' commutes. Whether drivers benefit is beside the point.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A new park won't help children, since adults are the ones who'll use the walking trails.

questions.stimulus: Veterinary researcher: Dogs fed from puzzle feeders, which make a dog work to get its food out, show fewer destructive behaviors at home than dogs fed from ordinary bowls. This suggests that the mental effort of working out food reduces the boredom that drives much destructive behavior in dogs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the veterinary researcher’s argument?
choices: Dogs switched from bowls to puzzle feeders showed fewer destructive behaviors over the following weeks.
Owners who buy puzzle feeders tend to spend more time exercising their dogs than other owners do.
Puzzle feeders slow down dogs’ eating, which can reduce some digestive problems.
Some dogs fed from puzzle feeders still chew furniture when left alone.
Destructive behavior is more common among some breeds of dogs than among others.
questions.explanation: The original evidence compares different dogs, so the difference might reflect the owners or the dogs rather than the feeders. (A) shows the same dogs improving after the switch, which makes the feeder a more likely cause. (B) offers a competing explanation and so weakens; (C) is tempting because it describes another effect of the feeders, but digestion has nothing to do with boredom-driven behavior.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mental effort of working food out of a puzzle feeder reduces the boredom that drives much destructive behavior in dogs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dogs fed from puzzle feeders show fewer destructive behaviors at home than dogs fed from ordinary bowls.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence compares different dogs with different owners. Maybe puzzle-feeder owners are just more attentive, or their dogs are calmer to begin with. The best strengthener isolates the feeder. One clean way: same dogs, before and after switching. If the same dog gets better after the switch, it's hard to blame the owner or the breed. Like testing new glasses: if you see better after putting them on, it wasn't your eyes changing.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same dogs, switched from bowls to puzzle feeders, fewer destructive behaviors afterward. That rules out "different dogs" or "different owners" as the explanation and makes the feeder look like the cause.
Weakens. Puzzle-feeder owners exercise their dogs more, and exercise could be why their dogs are less destructive. A rival cause.
Tempting because it's another real benefit of puzzle feeders. But digestion has nothing to do with boredom. Doesn't help the boredom explanation.
"Some" dogs still chew furniture. That's consistent with a reduction overall, and it if anything slightly hurts. Doesn't strengthen.
Breed differences only matter if the feeder group had different breeds, and this doesn't say so. At most it hints at a rival cause. Doesn't strengthen.

questions.stimulus: Astronomy club president: Some members want us to double the number of public stargazing nights, since attendance has been strong. But the program depends entirely on a handful of volunteers who bring and operate their own telescopes, and several of them say they are already stretched thin. Expanding in a way that drives those volunteers away would end the program altogether. So we should not double the number of nights.
questions.stem: The principle underlying the argument above is most similar to the principle underlying which one of the following arguments?
choices: Restaurant owner: Our lunch special is very popular, but we lose money on every one we serve. So we should raise its price, even if fewer customers order it.
School principal: Some parents want us to add field trips. But each trip uses money that would otherwise go to new books, and our book budget is already tight. So we should not add field trips.
Library director: Our volunteer tutors tell us they greatly enjoy their work. So we can extend tutoring hours without hiring any paid staff.

Garden coordinator: Neighbors want us to add a second garden plot. But our garden depends on a few retirees who already feel overworked, and if they quit there would be no garden at all. So we should not add the plot.
Mayor: The farmers market has become very crowded. It should move to a larger lot, even though vendors there would pay higher fees, because more customers would benefit the vendors as well.
questions.explanation: The president’s principle is that an activity should not be expanded if expanding it would likely drive off the few people it depends on and so end it entirely. (D) applies the same principle to a garden kept up by overworked retirees. (B) is the closest trap, but it rests on a budget tradeoff between two goods, not on losing the people who make the activity possible; (C) shares the volunteer theme but reaches the opposite kind of conclusion from a different consideration.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The club should not double the number of public stargazing nights.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The program depends entirely on a few volunteers who are already stretched thin; expanding in a way that drives them away would end the program.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: People want to expand X; X depends entirely on a few overstretched people; losing them would end X; so don't expand X.

breakdown.analysis: The principle: don't grow something if growing it would burn out the few people it can't survive without. Find the answer with the same logic: popular demand to expand, a small overworked group the whole thing depends on, and the risk of losing everything. Don't get pulled in by a choice that just says no to an expansion for some other reason.

choices.note: Different principle entirely: a money-losing item should have its price raised. No expansion request, no fragile group of people.
The closest trap. It also says "don't expand," but the reason is a budget tradeoff (field trips vs. books), not losing the people who keep the program alive.
Shares the volunteer theme but goes the other way: volunteers are happy, so expand. Different reasoning and opposite conclusion.
CORRECT. Neighbors want more; the garden depends on a few overworked retirees; if they quit there's no garden; so don't add the plot. Same principle, same structure.
This argues for expanding (moving to a bigger lot) based on benefits outweighing costs. Nothing about a small group of people the market depends on.

questions.stimulus: Office supply retailer: Of the customers who bought our Tallis desk chair last year, most also bought the optional lumbar cushion. Of the customers who returned the chair, most had not bought the cushion. No customer bought more than one chair.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most customers who did not buy the lumbar cushion returned the chair.
Buying the lumbar cushion made customers less likely to return the chair.
The return rate was higher among customers who skipped the cushion than among those who bought it.
More chairs were returned by customers who bought the lumbar cushion than by customers who did not buy it.
Most customers who bought the Tallis chair last year kept it.
questions.explanation: Customers without the cushion were the smaller group, yet they accounted for more of the returns, so their return rate must have been higher, which is (C). (B) is the most tempting choice, but the data show only a correlation; customers who skipped the cushion may differ in other ways, such as being less committed to the chair. (A) and (E) need information about the overall return rate, which is not given, and (D) contradicts the second statement.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Most Tallis chair buyers also bought the lumbar cushion; 2) most customers who returned the chair had not bought the cushion; 3) no one bought more than one chair.

breakdown.analysis: No-cushion buyers are the smaller group, but they make up most of the returns. A smaller group producing more returns has to have a higher return rate. Worked example: 100 buyers, 70 with cushion and 30 without. 10 returns, 6 from no-cushion buyers and 4 from cushion buyers. Return rates: 6/30 = 20% vs. 4/70 = about 6%. Any numbers that fit the facts give the same direction. But that's correlation, not cause.

choices.note: We don't know the overall return rate. If only 10 chairs came back out of 100, then only about 6 of 30 no-cushion buyers returned theirs. Not most.

Most tempting, but causal. The data show only that the two things go together. Maybe people who skipped the cushion were less committed to the chair from the start. Lesson: a higher rate in one group doesn't tell you why.
CORRECT. Smaller group, more returns → higher return rate. This is pure math from the first two facts and doesn't claim anything about cause.
Contradicts the second statement: most returns came from people who did not buy the cushion.
Needs the overall return rate, which we don't have. If 80% of chairs came back, both facts could still hold. Unsupported.

passages.title: Court-Appointed Expert Witnesses
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In most common-law jurisdictions a trial judge may, on a party’s motion or on the judge’s own initiative, appoint an expert witness of the court’s choosing. The power is seldom used, and its advocates attribute this to judicial timidity. There are, however, sound reasons for the reluctance.

First, an expert introduced to the jury as the court’s own arrives cloaked in a neutrality that no party’s expert can match. Jurors told that one witness was chosen by the judge are apt to treat that witness’s opinion not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified, so that a single person who was never meant to decide the case effectively does so.

Second, the appointment itself is far from neutral. In fields where the science is unsettled—the reliability of certain forensic techniques, say, or the causes of a rare illness—competent specialists disagree, and to select one of them is to select a side. A judge, who by hypothesis lacks the expertise to resolve the dispute, is poorly placed to recognize that a choice of person is also a choice of doctrine, and the jury will never learn that such a choice was made at all.

Third, the court’s expert is shielded from the testing that adversarial procedure supplies. A lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge’s own witness risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk. The remedy for partisan expertise is not to abandon the adversarial method but to strengthen it: earlier disclosure of expert reports, and pretrial hearings at which opposing experts must confront each other’s reasoning.

Passage B

Litigants do not hire experts at random. They interview several and retain the one whose views best serve their case—or whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it. The result in a technical dispute is often two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable, presented to jurors who have no basis for choosing between them. Research with mock jurors suggests that in such contests jurors tend to credit the expert who seems more poised and likable, a standard bearing little relation to the merits.

A court-appointed expert addresses this problem not by replacing the parties’ experts but by giving jurors a fixed point against which to measure them. The parties remain free to call their own witnesses and to cross-examine the court’s. And if jurors give the court’s expert more weight than either party’s, that is hardly a defect: an expert chosen for competence rather than for persuasiveness deserves more weight.

Nor need the selection be left to a judge’s unaided guesswork. Courts can ask each side to nominate candidates and appoint someone acceptable to both, or can request that a professional body propose a panel from which the judge chooses.
