Where a field is genuinely divided, the appointed expert can be instructed to report the range of respectable opinion rather than only her own. And the judge should tell jurors plainly that the court’s expert is a witness like any other, whose testimony they are free to accept or reject.

passages.title: Serial Publication and the Victorian Novel
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers began appearing in monthly parts in 1836, it helped establish a mode of publication that dominated British fiction for decades: novels issued in installments, as separate numbers or in magazines, over a year or more. The literary historian Ines Varga has argued that many of the features for which Victorian novels were long criticized are best understood as products of this mode. The suspenseful endings of installments, the proliferation of subplots, and the habit of tagging minor characters with a signature phrase or mannerism are, on Varga’s account, not lapses of craft but rational responses to what she calls “serial form.” She has little patience for earlier critics who dismissed such features as “padding paid for by the page,” a judgment she describes as mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures.

Varga’s account is persuasive in outline, but it fails to clarify what serial form is supposed to have demanded. In her usage the term does double duty. Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers, who met a novel in fragments weeks apart and so needed reminders of who was who and reasons to buy the next number. At other times it refers to the situation of writers, many of whom composed each installment shortly before it was due, could not revise chapters already in print, and learned of the public’s response while the story was still unfinished. These are distinct pressures, and they predict different things: the first should leave its mark wherever readers encountered a text intermittently, however it was written; the second, wherever a text was written under deadline, however it was read.

Varga’s evidence, moreover, rests on a comparison whose significance she does not establish. She shows that the features in question are markedly more common in serialized novels than in novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries. But the comparison is telling only if the two groups of novels are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are. If publishers offered serialization chiefly to established popular authors, whose habits of plotting predated their first serials, or to comic and sensational stories, in which suspense and broadly drawn minor characters were long-standing conventions, the difference she documents may owe less to the mode of publication than to the authors and stories it attracted.

The case of the novelist Edmund Carrow complicates matters further. Carrow, unusually, finished each of his novels before its first installment appeared, yet his books abound in cliffhangers and in minor characters identified by recurring tics. Varga treats Carrow as confirming her thesis, since he wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts. Perhaps so—but his novels contain almost none of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail that she also attributes to serial form. Carrow thus suggests that the two pressures her term conflates operated independently. Varga has identified a real cause; what her account needs is a finer description of how that cause worked.

passages.title: Unbalanced accounts in the Orlen Valley ledgers
passages.text:
When the household account books kept by farming families in the Orlen Valley between roughly 1780 and 1860 were first catalogued in the 1950s, archivists noticed a curious feature. Entries recording loans of grain, labor, and tools between neighboring households almost never balance. When such a debt was repaid, the repayment was nearly always a little more or a little less than the original loan, and the difference was carried forward rather than settled. Early commentators took this as evidence of careless bookkeeping, or of a rural population that lacked the arithmetic to reconcile its accounts.

The anthropologist Teodora Halvik has offered a different explanation. In her view, the imbalances were deliberate. Among Orlen households, she argues, an exchange that ended with nothing owed on either side ended the relationship as well; to repay a neighbor exactly was to announce that one no longer wished to be bound to that neighbor. Keeping a small remainder perpetually outstanding was thus a way of keeping the relationship open. Halvik notes that the ledgers have a local expression for such an account: it is said to be “on the long thread.”

Halvik’s evidence is of several kinds. The same households that left their neighbors’ accounts unbalanced kept precise records of their dealings with grain merchants from outside the valley, and those accounts were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete. Nor were the remainders random: they were small, typically less than a tenth of the original loan, and the direction of the imbalance tended to alternate, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor. Finally, in the few cases in which an account between neighbors was closed exactly, parish records from the same months frequently note a dispute between the two families, a lawsuit, or the departure of one of them from the valley.

The ledger of the Brenn household illustrates the mechanism. In the spring of 1812 the Brenns lent eight bushels of rye to the neighboring Tamm family. At harvest the Tamms returned nine, leaving the Brenns owing the Tamms one bushel. That winter the Brenns repaid the bushel with two days of labor on the Tamms’ threshing floor—work the ledger values at slightly more than a bushel, so that the Tamms now owed the Brenns a small fraction. The account continued in this way, alternating, for thirty-one years. It was closed only in 1843, the year in which the parish register records that a quarrel over a boundary stone had divided the two families.

If Halvik is right, the ledgers are not failed attempts at reckoning but successful records of a different kind: they tracked not merely what was owed but who remained bound to whom. Orlen arithmetic, on this account, was exact where exactness served a purpose and deliberately loose where looseness did.

passages.title: Recruitment failure in the slate pearlmussel
passages.text:
For most of the twentieth century, the slate pearlmussel was among the most abundant freshwater mussels in the Halder River. By the 1970s, however, surveys upstream of the Ostrow Dam, completed in 1931, were finding fewer of the mussels each decade, and the decline was attributed to the industrial pollution and agricultural sediment that had degraded much of the river. A regional cleanup program begun in 1978 cut discharges sharply, and by the late 1980s water quality above the dam met every standard the program had set. The mussels continued to decline.

In 1994 the biologist Renata Kovač proposed that the problem lay not in the water but in the mussel’s life cycle. Like many freshwater mussels, the slate pearlmussel cannot complete its development on its own. A female releases larvae, called glochidia, that must clamp onto the gills of a fish, where they become encapsulated in its tissue and live as parasites for several weeks before dropping off as juvenile mussels. Kovač found that glochidia exposed in the laboratory to a dozen fish species transformed successfully only on the Halder herring, a migratory fish that once ascended the river each spring to spawn; on other species they were shed within days. The dam, which had no fish passage, had ended the herring’s runs. Kovač then aged living mussels by counting the annual growth rings on their shells. Downstream of the dam, mussels of every age were present; upstream, nearly all were more than sixty years old—older, that is, than the dam itself. Because adults can live for most of a century, she argued, the upstream population had been reproductively dead for decades while appearing merely diminished.

Kovač urged that funds be redirected from further water-quality measures to fish passage at the dam, and her proposal met resistance. Some biologists objected that laboratory results might not reflect conditions in the river, where glochidia might use hosts that fare poorly in tanks. Others noted that the dam had also caused fine sediment to accumulate above it, and that juvenile mussels, which burrow and feed in the riverbed, are more sensitive to such sediment than adults are. The missing age classes, these critics argued, might reflect where juveniles could survive rather than whether they were being produced.

A fish lift began operating at the dam in 2008. Within two years, herring caught upstream were found carrying encysted glochidia, and surveys in 2015 recovered juvenile pearlmussels above the dam for the first time in living memory—including in reaches where sediment had not measurably changed. Recruitment was nonetheless markedly lower in the siltiest reaches, suggesting that Kovač’s critics had identified a real, though secondary, constraint. The episode is now often cited as a caution: a population of long-lived adults can conceal a failure of reproduction for generations.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes the historical development of a procedural power, while passage B evaluates several proposals for reforming that power.
Passage A and passage B both criticize a procedural power, but they propose different remedies for the defects each identifies in it.
Passage A argues that a procedural power should be used more often, while passage B argues that it should be reserved for unusually technical disputes.
Passage A argues against the use of a procedural power, while passage B argues for its use and proposes measures that bear on some problems passage A raises.
Passage A identifies problems with a procedural power, while passage B argues that those problems are less serious than the problems with every alternative to it.
questions.explanation: Passage A gives three reasons for judges' reluctance to appoint their own experts and recommends strengthening adversarial testing instead; passage B defends court-appointed experts and offers safeguards (joint nomination, professional panels, a range-of-opinion report, a jury instruction) that answer A's worries about selection and deference, so D is correct. E is the most tempting trap: B argues that dueling party experts are a serious problem, but it never surveys 'every alternative' and never considers A's proposed reform. B misreads passage B as critical, and C reverses passage A's stance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the two passages relate: A's stance on court-appointed experts, B's stance, and how B's proposals line up with A's worries.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1 ('sound reasons for the reluctance') and its three numbered objections. Passage B, paragraphs 2-3 (the case for appointment and the safeguards: joint nomination, professional panels, range-of-opinion reports, a jury instruction).

breakdown.analysis: A: judges are right to rarely appoint their own experts; three reasons (jurors defer, selection picks a side, cross-examination gets chilled); fix the adversarial system instead. B: party experts are bought and jurors pick the likable one; a court expert gives jurors a fixed point; and here's how to make selection fair and tell the jury the expert is just a witness. B's safeguards speak to A's selection and deference worries. Prephrase: A is against, B is for and offers fixes that address some of A's concerns.

choices.note: A isn't history. It's an argument against using the power. And B doesn't weigh several reform proposals; it argues for using the power, with safeguards.
Misreads B. B defends the power. It isn't a critic proposing a different remedy.
Reverses A. A defends judges' reluctance to use the power. And B doesn't limit it to unusually technical disputes.

CORRECT. A argues against the power and prefers strengthening adversarial testing. B argues for it and proposes measures (joint nomination, professional panels, range-of-opinion reports, a jury instruction) that respond to A's worries about biased selection and juror deference.

The trap. B does think dueling party experts are a serious problem, but it never surveys 'every alternative' and never considers A's proposed reform (earlier disclosure, pretrial confrontation). 'Every alternative' is far beyond what B does.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B?
choices: the possibility that a judge could ask a professional body to propose candidates for appointment
the reluctance of attorneys to cross-examine forcefully a witness whom the judge has chosen
the existence of technical fields in which competent specialists disagree with one another
the tendency of jurors to credit whichever of two experts seems more poised and likable
the right of parties to present their own experts even when the court has appointed one
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says a lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge's witness 'risks appearing to quarrel with the judge'; passage B says only that parties 'remain free' to cross-examine the court's expert, which is a point about permission, not reluctance, so B is correct. C is the likeliest trap, but it appears in both passages (A's 'competent specialists disagree'; B's 'Where a field is genuinely divided'). A, D, and E appear only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the item that shows up in passage A and does not show up in passage B. Check each choice against both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 4 (lawyers risk 'appearing to quarrel with the judge'). Passage B, paragraph 2 ('The parties remain free ... to cross-examine the court's').

breakdown.analysis: This is a two-part check: is it in A, and is it missing from B? Run each choice through both. The answer is A's point that lawyers are reluctant to cross-examine the judge's own witness aggressively. B mentions cross-examination too, but only as something parties are free to do. That's permission, not reluctance. The lesson: a shared topic isn't a shared claim. Being allowed to do something and being willing to do it are different points.

choices.note: Only in B (paragraph 3: a professional body could propose a panel). A never suggests it.

CORRECT. A says a lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge's witness 'risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk.' B only says parties 'remain free' to cross-examine, which is about permission, not reluctance.
The likeliest trap, because it's clearly in A ('competent specialists disagree'). But it's in B too: 'Where a field is genuinely divided.' So it fails the 'not in B' half.
Only in B. The mock-juror research on poised, likable experts is in B's first paragraph.
Only in B ('The parties remain free to call their own witnesses'). A never makes this point.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that some experts retained by litigants are too
choices: accommodating
cautious
specialized
numerous
inexpensive
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of passage B says litigants retain the expert whose views 'for an adequate fee, can be made to serve' their case, implying that some experts are too willing to fit their views to the party paying them: too accommodating (A). E inverts the reference to fees, which concerns experts' willingness to be paid for favorable views, not their cost; B, C, and D have no support in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer the flaw passage B attributes to some experts hired by litigants. Pick the one word that fits.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1: litigants retain the expert 'whose views best serve their case—or whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it.'

breakdown.analysis: The key phrase is 'for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it.' That describes experts who will bend their opinions to suit whoever's paying. Prephrase: too willing to go along, too pliable. The fee is about their willingness to be paid for favorable views, not about their price.

choices.note: CORRECT. Experts whose views 'can be made to serve' a case 'for an adequate fee' are too willing to fit their opinions to the client. That's too accommodating.
No support. B describes the experts as 'confident,' not cautious, and the problem is that they bend, not that they hold back.
Nothing in B says they're too narrow in expertise. The complaint is about bias, not specialization.
B says litigants interview several experts, but the problem isn't that there are too many experts. It's how the chosen one's views get shaped.
Inverts the fee reference. 'For an adequate fee' is about experts being paid to tailor their views, not about them being cheap.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: jurors are likely to give the testimony of a court-appointed expert more weight than the testimony of a party’s expert
parties should be permitted to cross-examine an expert whom the court has appointed
competent specialists sometimes reach conflicting conclusions on technical questions
the testimony of experts retained by litigants tends to reflect the interests of those litigants
the weight jurors are likely to give a court-appointed expert’s testimony is a reason against appointing such experts
questions.explanation: Passage A's first objection is that jurors will treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'; passage B replies that if jurors give that expert more weight, 'that is hardly a defect,' since an expert chosen for competence deserves it. They thus disagree about whether such deference counts against appointment (E). A is the strong trap: passage B does not deny that jurors will give the court's expert more weight (its 'if' clause concedes the possibility), so the disagreement is about the significance of that weight, not its existence. C and D are points both authors accept, and B is something passage A never addresses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a point where the two authors would take opposite sides: one says yes, the other says no.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2 (jurors treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'). Passage B, paragraph 2 ('if jurors give the court's expert more weight ... that is hardly a defect').

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. A's first objection: jurors will over-weight the court's expert, so a single person effectively decides the case. That's a reason not to appoint. B: if jurors give that expert more weight, 'that is hardly a defect,' because an expert chosen for competence deserves it. They might agree that jurors give more weight; they split on whether that's a reason against appointment. Prephrase: whether the extra weight jurors give the court's expert counts against appointing one.

choices.note: The strong trap. A says yes. But B doesn't say no: its 'if' clause allows that jurors may give more weight, and it argues that this is fine. Their fight is over what that weight means, not whether it happens.
A never addresses whether cross-examination should be permitted; it talks about lawyers' reluctance. B says it's allowed. No clear clash.
Both agree. A: 'competent specialists disagree.' B: 'Where a field is genuinely divided.'
Both would likely agree. A calls it 'partisan expertise' that needs a remedy; B says experts are retained because their views serve the case.

CORRECT. A treats jurors' deference to the court's expert as a reason against appointment: the expert becomes 'a verdict to be ratified.' B says that extra weight is 'hardly a defect.' One says it counts against appointment; the other says it doesn't.

questions.stem: The relationship between passage A and passage B is most analogous to the relationship between the documents described in which one of the following?
choices: an essay titled “Why Arbitrators Should Rely on the Parties’ Rival Appraisals” and an essay titled “Improving the Exchange of Appraisal Reports Before Arbitration Hearings”
an essay titled “In Defense of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “The Dangers of Letting Arbitrators Choose Their Own Appraisers”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “How Parties to Arbitration Can Choose Better Appraisers of Their Own”
an essay titled “A Short History of Appraisal in Commercial Arbitration” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
questions.explanation: Passage A criticizes a decision maker's appointing its own supposedly neutral expert, and passage B defends that practice as giving decision makers a fixed point between rival partisan experts; C reproduces both stances and B's 'fixed point' rationale. B reverses the order of the two stances. D is the closest trap: its first title matches passage A, but its second is about improving the parties' own experts, which is closer to passage A's remedy than to passage B's defense. A has two essays favoring the adversarial approach, and E's first essay is historical rather than critical.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Analogy: find a pair of essay titles whose relationship matches A-then-B. Order and stance both matter.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A's overall stance (paragraph 1: reasons against appointment). Passage B's central rationale (paragraph 2: 'a fixed point against which to measure them').

breakdown.analysis: Turn the passages into titles. A: 'Problems with Judges Picking Their Own Experts.' B: 'The Case for Court-Appointed Experts as a Reference Point Between Partisan Experts.' Now look for that pattern in arbitration: first essay against the decision maker's own appraiser, second for it, ideally with the benchmark idea. The lesson: on paired-passage analogy questions, check direction (order of stances) as well as subject.

choices.note: Both essays favor the adversarial approach (rely on rival appraisals; improve report exchange). That's roughly two versions of A, and there's no B-style defense.
Right stances, wrong order. The first essay defends the practice and the second attacks it. That's B then A.

CORRECT. First essay: the hidden hazards of arbitrator-commissioned appraisals, matching A's objections. Second: a benchmark between rival valuations, the case for arbitrator-commissioned appraisals, matching B's defense and its 'fixed point' rationale.

The closest trap. The first title matches A. But the second is about helping parties pick better appraisers of their own, which is closer to A's remedy (strengthen the adversarial side) than to B's defense of a decision maker's own expert.
The second title fits B, but the first is a history, not a critique. A argues; it doesn't narrate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in passage B that judges tell jurors the court’s expert is a witness like any other?
choices: Jurors who know that the judge selected the expert are likely to go on treating that expert’s opinion as authoritative regardless of what they are told.
Such an instruction would discourage jurors from giving the court’s expert the additional weight that the expert’s neutrality warrants.
Such an instruction would reveal to jurors a fact about how the expert was selected that they would otherwise never learn.
Such an instruction would make attorneys more willing to cross-examine the court’s expert aggressively, needlessly prolonging trials.
Such an instruction would be unnecessary, since jurors already regard the court’s expert as no more reliable than other witnesses.
questions.explanation: Passage A's first objection is that jurors told a witness was chosen by the judge treat that witness's opinion 'not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified'; an instruction that leaves jurors knowing who chose the expert would not dispel that aura, so A is correct. B states passage B's view of the expert's added weight, not passage A's. C is tempting because passage A says the jury 'will never learn' something, but that refers to the choice of doctrine, and passage A assumes jurors are told who chose the witness. D and E conflict with passage A's own concerns.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage A's author would criticize B's proposal that judges tell jurors the court's expert is a witness like any other.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 3 (last sentence: the jury instruction). Passage A, paragraph 2 (jurors told a witness was chosen by the judge treat that opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified').

breakdown.analysis: A's first objection isn't about anything the judge says about the witness. It's about the fact jurors know: the judge chose this person. That knowledge cloaks the expert in neutrality, and jurors treat the opinion as a verdict to ratify. B's instruction still tells jurors it's 'the court's expert,' so the aura stays. Prephrase: telling jurors to treat the expert like anyone else won't work; knowing the judge picked the expert will still make them defer. It's like a boss saying 'my nephew's opinion counts the same as yours' in a meeting. Everyone still knows whose nephew he is.

choices.note: CORRECT. A says jurors who know the judge chose a witness treat that witness's opinion 'not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified.' An instruction that still identifies the expert as the court's own won't undo that, so A would say jurors will keep treating it as authoritative.
That's B's view (a competent expert 'deserves more weight'), not A's. A thinks the extra weight is the problem, so A wouldn't complain that the instruction reduces it.

Tempting because A says the jury 'will never learn' something. But that's about the choice of doctrine hidden in picking an expert, not who picked the expert. A assumes jurors are told the judge chose the witness.
A's concern is that lawyers are too reluctant to cross-examine the court's expert. A would welcome more aggressive cross-examination, not complain that it prolongs trials.
Directly against A, which says jurors treat the court's expert as more authoritative, not as no more reliable than other witnesses.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the remedy proposed in the last sentence of passage A as inadequate on the grounds that it
choices: would deprive the parties of the opportunity to cross-examine opposing experts in the presence of the jury
would leave jurors without an independent reference point for assessing the conflicting conclusions of the parties’ experts
presupposes that judges can choose qualified experts competently without the assistance of the parties
would make litigants’ selection of experts whose views serve their case even more strategic than it already is
would require jurors to master the technical reasoning that the opposing experts present at pretrial hearings
questions.explanation: Passage B locates the problem in jurors having 'no basis for choosing between' two partisan experts, and it presents the court's expert as 'a fixed point against which to measure them'; passage A's remedy (earlier disclosure and pretrial confrontation between the parties' experts) still leaves only partisan experts, so B is correct. C is the most tempting trap because it echoes passage B's phrase 'unaided guesswork,' but passage A's remedy involves no judicial selection of experts at all. E misplaces the jury at pretrial hearings, and A and D have no basis in either passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict why passage B's author would think passage A's proposed remedy falls short.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 4, last sentence (earlier disclosure of expert reports; pretrial hearings where opposing experts confront each other). Passage B, paragraph 1 (jurors have 'no basis for choosing') and paragraph 2 ('a fixed point against which to measure them').

breakdown.analysis: B's diagnosis: jurors face two confident partisan experts and have no basis for choosing between them, so they go with the more likable one. B's cure: a neutral fixed point. A's remedy only sharpens the contest between the two partisan experts. There's still no independent reference point for jurors. Prephrase: A's fix leaves jurors without a neutral benchmark. Match the criticism to what B actually cares about.

choices.note: No basis. A's remedy adds pretrial hearings; it doesn't take away cross-examination at trial. Neither passage says it would.

CORRECT. B's core problem is that jurors have 'no basis for choosing between' partisan experts, and its solution is 'a fixed point against which to measure them.' A's remedy still leaves only partisan experts, so the reference point is still missing.
The most tempting trap, since it echoes B's 'unaided guesswork.' But A's remedy doesn't involve a judge selecting any expert, so this criticism doesn't apply to it.
Neither passage suggests A's remedy would make litigants more strategic in hiring experts. Pure speculation.
Misplaces the jury. Pretrial hearings happen before trial, between the experts. Nothing says jurors must attend or master that reasoning.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Varga has shown that features of Victorian novels that earlier critics dismissed as flaws of craft were in fact rational responses to the demands of serial publication.
Varga’s account of the influence of serial publication on the Victorian novel is undermined by the case of a novelist who completed his books before serializing them.
Although Varga is right that serial publication shaped the Victorian novel, her account conflates distinct pressures and rests on a comparison of uncertain significance.
The features of Victorian serialized novels are better explained by the pressures that serial publication placed on writers than by those it placed on readers.
Varga’s comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete overlooks differences between the kinds of authors and stories in the two groups.
questions.explanation: The author calls Varga's account 'persuasive in outline' and concludes that she 'has identified a real cause,' while the second and fourth paragraphs show that her term conflates two pressures and the third questions her comparison, so C is correct. A states Varga's view without the author's reservations. B overstates the author's attitude toward the Carrow case, which complicates rather than refutes her thesis. D picks one pressure over the other, whereas the author says both operated. E is a single point from the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point: the author's overall verdict on Varga's account of serial form.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first sentence ('persuasive in outline, but it fails to clarify ...') and paragraph 4, last sentence ('Varga has identified a real cause; what her account needs is a finer description ...').

breakdown.analysis: The author's frame is 'right in outline, needs refining.' Paragraph 2: her term conflates two pressures, on readers and on writers. Paragraph 3: her key comparison assumes the two groups of novels are otherwise alike. Paragraph 4: Carrow shows the two pressures worked independently. And the conclusion: she found 'a real cause' but needs a finer account. Prephrase: Varga is right that serialization mattered, but she blurs two pressures and leans on a shaky comparison. A main-point answer has to include both the endorsement and the criticisms.

choices.note: Varga's view without the author's reservations. The author calls it only 'persuasive in outline' and spends three paragraphs on its problems.
Overstates the Carrow case. The author says it 'complicates matters,' not that it undermines her account, and still says she identified 'a real cause.'

CORRECT. 'Right that serial publication shaped the Victorian novel' matches 'persuasive in outline' and 'a real cause.' 'Conflates distinct pressures' is paragraphs 2 and 4. 'A comparison of uncertain significance' is paragraph 3.
The author doesn't pick a winner. The point is that both pressures operated and Varga's term blurs them, not that writers' pressure explains more.
Accurate, but it's only paragraph 3. A main point has to cover the whole passage, including the conflation problem and the overall 'real cause' verdict.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s attitude toward the judgment of earlier critics that certain features of Victorian novels were “padding paid for by the page” can best be described as one of
choices: indifference
sympathy
ambivalence
deference
disapproval
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says Varga 'has little patience' for those critics and describes their judgment as 'mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures,' which is disapproval (E). C is the likeliest trap for readers who notice that the author has reservations about Varga, but those reservations are the author's, not Varga's, and Varga herself is not described as torn about the critics' judgment. A, B, and D are contradicted by her impatience with them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe Varga's attitude (not the author's) toward the earlier critics' 'padding paid for by the page' judgment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence: 'She has little patience for earlier critics ... a judgment she describes as mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures.'

breakdown.analysis: 'Little patience' plus calling their judgment a mistake. That's clearly negative. Prephrase: disapproval. Keep the speakers straight: the author has mixed feelings about Varga, but this question is about Varga's feelings toward the critics.

choices.note: Contradicted. 'Little patience' isn't indifference. She cares enough to call their judgment a mistake.
Opposite. She rejects their judgment.
The likeliest trap. Someone in the passage is mixed, but that's the author about Varga. Varga herself is never described as torn about the critics.
Opposite. Deference would mean accepting their judgment; she says they mistook 'the conditions of an art for its failures.'
CORRECT. 'Little patience' and calling their view a mistake both signal disapproval.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “does double duty” (second sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that Varga’s term “serial form”
choices: serves both to explain certain features of Victorian novels and to defend those features against earlier critics
covers both publication in separate numbers and publication in magazines
is used both by Varga and by the earlier critics whose judgments about the novels she rejects
is applied, without distinction, to two different sets of circumstances that might have shaped the novels
names both the characteristic features of serialized novels and the conditions that produced those features
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the phrase: 'sometimes' the term refers to readers' situation and 'at other times' to writers', and the author calls these 'distinct pressures,' so D is correct. A is the strongest trap because Varga's account does both explain and defend the features, but the second paragraph is about what the term refers to, not about the uses of her account. B draws on the two formats mentioned in the first paragraph, which the author never says the term blurs. C and E have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the author means by saying Varga's term 'serial form' 'does double duty.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the sentences right after the phrase: 'Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers ... At other times it refers to the situation of writers ...' and 'These are distinct pressures.'

breakdown.analysis: The author defines the phrase right away: 'serial form' sometimes means the readers' situation (fragments weeks apart) and sometimes the writers' situation (deadlines, no revision, live feedback). Those are 'distinct pressures' that predict different things, and Varga uses one term for both. Prephrase: the term covers two different sets of conditions without separating them. On meaning-in-context questions, the next sentence is usually the definition.

choices.note: The strongest trap. Varga's account does both explain and defend the features. But the 'double duty' passage is about what the term refers to (readers or writers), not the two jobs her account performs.
Borrows paragraph 1's two formats (separate numbers, magazines). The author never says the term blurs those.
No support. The earlier critics said 'padding paid for by the page'; nothing says they used the term 'serial form.'
CORRECT. The term 'sometimes' means readers' situation and 'at other times' writers'. The author calls them 'distinct pressures,' and Varga applies one term to both without distinguishing them.
Not what the passage says. Both senses the author identifies are conditions (readers' and writers' situations), not one condition and one set of features.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: distinguish two senses of a term that is used in the first paragraph
identify an assumption relied upon by the evidence offered for the view described in the first paragraph
present a case that the view described in the first paragraph is unable to accommodate
explain why the critics mentioned in the first paragraph regarded certain features of novels as flaws
offer evidence that conclusively refutes the view described in the first paragraph
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Varga's comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete 'is telling only if the two groups of novels are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are,' and then shows how the groups might differ, so B is correct. A describes the second paragraph and C the fourth (and even the Carrow case is presented as a complication, not as something Varga cannot accommodate). E is too strong: the paragraph raises possibilities introduced by 'if' and says the difference 'may' have another source.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: what is the third paragraph's role in the passage?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: 'the comparison is telling only if the two groups of novels are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are.'

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3 takes Varga's evidence (features are more common in serialized novels than in three-volume novels) and points out the hidden assumption: the two groups are alike in every other way. Then it shows how they might not be (established authors, comic and sensational genres). Prephrase: it exposes an assumption Varga's evidence depends on. It's like saying people who take vitamins are healthier, so vitamins work, while ignoring that vitamin-takers also exercise more.

choices.note: That's paragraph 2's job, the 'double duty' discussion of readers versus writers.
CORRECT. The paragraph names an assumption Varga's comparison relies on ('Varga simply assumes that they are' otherwise alike) and shows why it might fail.
That's closer to paragraph 4 (Carrow), and even there the case is presented as a complication, not something Varga can't handle. Paragraph 3 raises no particular case.
Paragraph 3 doesn't explain the earlier critics at all. They appear only in paragraph 1.
Too strong. The paragraph speaks in 'if' and says the difference 'may' have another source. It raises doubt; it doesn't conclusively refute anything.

questions.stem: The author mentions “comic and sensational stories” (last sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: indicate one way in which serialized novels might have differed from novels first issued complete other than in their mode of publication
identify the kinds of fiction for which publishers first adopted the practice of issuing novels in installments
suggest that the earlier critics’ dismissal of certain features as padding was justified for some kinds of fiction
illustrate the pressures that serial publication placed on readers who encountered novels in fragments
show that suspenseful endings were more common in novels issued complete than in serialized novels
questions.explanation: The reference appears in an 'if' clause describing ways the two groups of novels Varga compares might not be 'otherwise alike': if serialization went chiefly to genres in which suspense and broadly drawn characters were already conventions, the difference she documents could reflect genre rather than publication mode. That is A. D is tempting because suspense and memorable minor characters relate to readers' needs, but the point here concerns the composition of the comparison groups. B attributes a historical claim the passage never makes, and C and E are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: why does the author mention 'comic and sensational stories'?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence: the 'If publishers offered serialization chiefly to ... comic and sensational stories' clause.

breakdown.analysis: The phrase sits inside an 'if' clause that lists ways the serialized group and the complete-volume group might differ besides how they were published. If serials were mostly comic or sensational, the suspense and broad minor characters might come from the genre, not the format. Prephrase: it's one possible difference between the two groups other than publication mode. The 'if' tells you it's a hypothetical confounder, not a historical claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. It's one of two possible confounders: serialized novels might differ from complete novels in genre, and genre conventions, not publication mode, could explain Varga's results.
Turns a hypothetical into history. The passage says 'if' publishers offered serialization chiefly to such stories; it never says they first did.
Unsupported. The point isn't that the critics were right about padding. It's about what Varga's comparison can prove.
Tempting, since suspense and memorable minor characters relate to readers' needs. But here the point is about which novels ended up in each comparison group, not about readers' pressure.
No support. Nothing says suspense was more common in complete novels. Varga's data say the reverse, and the author doesn't dispute the data.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s interpretation of Carrow’s novels commits her to which one of the following views?
choices: Carrow’s novels contain the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail typical of serialized fiction.
The pressures that serial publication placed on readers and on writers operated independently of each other.
The term “serial form” should be used to refer only to the situation of readers who met novels in installments.
Some of the features she attributes to serial form can arise in a novel whose author did not compose it under installment deadlines.
Novelists who completed their work before serialization were more skilled at plotting than those who wrote installment by installment.
questions.explanation: Carrow finished each novel before serialization, so he did not write under installment deadlines, yet Varga treats his cliffhangers and recurring tics as confirming her thesis; she must therefore hold that features she attributes to serial form can arise without deadline composition (D). B is the most tempting trap, but it is the author's conclusion from the Carrow case, not something Varga's reading requires; the passage says her term 'conflates' the two pressures. C is too strong, since accepting reader-side effects in Carrow does not commit her to dropping the writer-side sense of the term. A is contradicted by the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what view Varga is committed to by treating Carrow as confirming her thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: Carrow 'finished each of his novels before its first installment appeared,' yet his books have cliffhangers and tics, and 'Varga treats Carrow as confirming her thesis.'

breakdown.analysis: Facts: Carrow wrote everything before serialization, so no deadline pressure. His novels still have cliffhangers and recurring tics, features Varga credits to serial form. She counts him as confirmation because readers met his work in parts. So she has to accept that some serial-form features can show up without deadline writing. Prephrase: some features she credits to serial form can arise even when the author didn't write under installment deadlines. Keep Varga's commitments separate from the author's conclusions.

choices.note: Contradicted. The passage says Carrow's novels contain 'almost none of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail.'
The most tempting trap. That's the author's conclusion from Carrow ('the two pressures her term conflates operated independently'). Varga's reading doesn't require it; her term conflates the two.
Too strong. Accepting reader-side effects in Carrow doesn't commit her to dropping the writer-side meaning of the term.

CORRECT. Carrow had no installment deadlines, yet Varga counts his cliffhangers and tics as serial-form features. So she's committed to the view that some of those features can arise without deadline composition.
Nothing about skill. The passage compares the presence of features, not which novelists plotted better.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if discovered, would provide the strongest evidence that the conditions under which serial novelists wrote, independently of the conditions under which their readers read, produced some of the features Varga attributes to serial form?
choices: A novelist who completed each of her novels before serialization nonetheless ended nearly every installment with a suspenseful scene.
Novels written month by month for serial publication contain more cliffhangers, subplots, and recurring tics than do novels first issued complete.

A novel delivered to its publisher chapter by chapter against monthly deadlines, but always intended to be issued only in complete form, contains many abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail.
Readers of serialized novels often wrote to the authors complaining that they had forgotten who the minor characters were between installments.
A novel composed slowly over several years and first issued in complete form contains few abandoned subplots or inconsistencies of detail.
questions.explanation: To isolate the writers' pressure, a case must have deadline composition without intermittent reading; C supplies exactly that, and the features it shows (abandoned subplots, inconsistencies) are the ones the fourth paragraph links to writers rather than readers. E is the most tempting trap: it fits the writer-side account, but its novel lacks both deadline composition and intermittent reading, so it cannot tell the two pressures apart. A is a Carrow-like case that isolates the readers' pressure, B is Varga's own undifferentiated comparison, and D concerns readers' needs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the evidence that best shows writers' conditions, on their own and apart from readers' conditions, produced some serial-form features.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (writers' pressure 'should leave its mark ... wherever a text was written under deadline, however it was read') and paragraph 4 (abandoned subplots and inconsistencies as the features Carrow lacks).

breakdown.analysis: To isolate a cause, you need a case with that cause and without the other. Here: written under deadline, but not read in pieces. If that case still shows serial-type features, the writers' pressure did it alone. And the best features to look for are the ones the passage ties to writers: abandoned subplots and inconsistencies, which Carrow (no deadlines) lacked. Prephrase: a deadline-written novel published only complete that still has abandoned subplots and inconsistencies. This is the classic control-group move: change one variable, hold the other fixed.

choices.note: Backwards. A Carrow-like case: no deadlines, read in parts. It isolates the readers' pressure, not the writers'.
Varga's original comparison. Serialized novels had both pressures at once, so this can't tell them apart.

CORRECT. Chapter-by-chapter deadlines (writers' pressure) but issued only complete (no readers' pressure), and it still has abandoned subplots and inconsistencies, the features paragraph 4 links to writing under deadline. That isolates the writers' conditions.
About readers' needs (forgetting minor characters between installments). It supports the readers' side, not the writers'.

The most tempting trap. It's consistent with the writer-side story (no deadlines, few inconsistencies), but this novel also lacks intermittent reading. It's missing both pressures, so it can't tell you which one matters.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Orlen Valley ledgers show that rural households of the period lacked the arithmetic needed to reconcile accounts with their neighbors.
Orlen Valley households kept careful accounts with outside merchants because they distrusted merchants more than they distrusted their neighbors.
The persistent imbalances in Orlen Valley accounts between neighbors, once attributed to poor bookkeeping, may instead have been a deliberate means of keeping relationships between households open.
The account between the Brenn and Tamm households shows that disputes between Orlen families were usually caused by the closing of an account.
Parish records demonstrate that whenever an Orlen household repaid a neighbor exactly, a quarrel between the two families followed.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle (paragraph 1), presents Halvik's explanation (paragraph 2), and supports it with evidence and an example, concluding that the ledgers may record who remained bound to whom; C captures this, including the author's hedged 'If Halvik is right.' A is the early commentators' view that the passage rejects. D is the most tempting trap: the Brenn account is only an illustration, and it shows the closing coinciding with a quarrel, not causing one, let alone that this was usual; E is too extreme ('whenever') given that the records only 'frequently' note disputes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point of the whole passage: the puzzle, Halvik's answer, and how firmly the author holds it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the imbalances and the 'careless bookkeeping' reading), paragraph 2 (Halvik: the imbalances were deliberate), and paragraph 5 ('If Halvik is right ...').

breakdown.analysis: Structure: puzzle (accounts between neighbors never balance), old explanation (sloppy bookkeeping), Halvik's new explanation (deliberate, to keep relationships open), evidence, an example, and a hedged wrap-up ('If Halvik is right'). Prephrase: the imbalances once blamed on poor bookkeeping may have been a deliberate way to keep households bound together. Note the hedge: the author presents Halvik's view sympathetically but doesn't declare it proven.

choices.note: That's the early commentators' view, the one the passage sets up to replace. Paragraph 5 also says Orlen arithmetic 'was exact where exactness served a purpose.'
The merchant accounts are evidence, not the point. And the passage never says households distrusted merchants; the contrast shows they could balance accounts when they wanted to.

CORRECT. Puzzle, old explanation, new explanation, and the hedge: 'once attributed to poor bookkeeping, may instead have been a deliberate means of keeping relationships ... open.' 'May' matches 'If Halvik is right.'
The most tempting trap. The Brenn account is one illustration, and it shows the closing coinciding with a quarrel, not causing one. 'Usually' turns a single case into a general rule.
Too extreme. Parish records 'frequently' note disputes when accounts closed exactly. 'Whenever ... followed' adds 'always' and a cause-then-effect order the passage doesn't give.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “on the long thread” (last sentence of the second paragraph), the ledgers most probably refer to
choices: an account between neighbors that has been deliberately left unsettled so that the obligation between them continues
a debt that has gone unpaid for so long that the creditor has given up hope of repayment
an account kept over many years with a grain merchant from outside the valley
a chain of borrowing in which a single loan passed through many households in turn
a record whose errors were too numerous for the bookkeeper to reconcile
questions.explanation: Halvik cites the expression as the local name for 'such an account', i.e., one in which a small remainder is kept 'perpetually outstanding' to keep the relationship open (paragraph 2); that is A. B is tempting because the account is long-lived, but nothing suggests repayment was hoped for and abandoned; the remainder was intended to stay open. C reverses the evidence, since merchant accounts were closed exactly, and E is the early commentators' reading Halvik rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the local expression 'on the long thread' refers to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: 'Keeping a small remainder perpetually outstanding was thus a way of keeping the relationship open. Halvik notes that the ledgers have a local expression for such an account ...'

breakdown.analysis: 'Such an account' points back to the previous sentence: an account with a small remainder deliberately kept outstanding to keep the relationship open. Prephrase: a deliberately unsettled account that keeps the neighbors bound. When a phrase is introduced with 'such,' look at what came just before.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Such an account' is the one with a small remainder 'perpetually outstanding' as 'a way of keeping the relationship open.' That's a deliberately unsettled account that keeps the obligation alive.
Tempting because the account is long-lived. But nobody gave up on repayment. Repayments kept happening; the remainder was left on purpose.
Reverses the evidence. Merchant accounts were closed 'to the last measure.' They were the opposite of a long thread.
Nothing about a loan passing through many households. The long thread is between two households.
That's the early commentators' reading (careless bookkeeping), which Halvik rejects.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the accounts that Orlen households kept with grain merchants from outside the valley
choices: were kept less carefully than the households' accounts with their neighbors
were often left with small remainders whose direction alternated over time
were the only ledger entries that archivists catalogued in the 1950s
were closed exactly whenever a transaction was complete
frequently gave rise to disputes that were recorded in parish registers
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that these accounts 'were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete,' which is D. B attributes the features of neighbors' accounts to merchants' accounts, and A reverses the contrast the passage draws. E transfers the parish-record evidence, which concerns neighbors' accounts that were closed exactly, to the merchant accounts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail question: what does the passage say about Orlen households' accounts with outside grain merchants?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence: those accounts 'were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete.'

breakdown.analysis: One sentence: households kept precise records with merchants and closed them exactly when each transaction finished. Prephrase: they were closed exactly. The traps take features of neighbor accounts (remainders, alternation, disputes) and pin them on merchant accounts.

choices.note: Reverses the contrast. Merchant accounts were kept precisely; it's the neighbor accounts that looked careless.
Those are features of the neighbor accounts, moved onto the merchant accounts.
No support. Archivists catalogued the account books generally; nothing says merchant entries were the only ones.
CORRECT. Paragraph 3: they 'were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete.'
Moves the parish-record evidence to the wrong accounts. The disputes in parish records concern neighbor accounts that were closed exactly.

questions.stem: If Halvik’s theory is correct, which one of the following would be most likely to have been true of a household that had newly settled in the Orlen Valley during the period in which the ledgers were kept?
choices: It would have avoided borrowing from its neighbors until it had established accounts with outside merchants.
If it wished to establish lasting ties with a neighbor, it would have repaid its first loan from that neighbor with slightly more or slightly less than it had borrowed.
It would have been expected to repay each neighbor exactly until the neighbor had extended it a second loan.
It would have kept its accounts with neighbors in a different measure from the one it used with outside merchants.
It would have been unable to borrow grain from neighbors without first performing labor for them.
questions.explanation: On Halvik's theory, exact repayment signaled a wish to end a relationship and a small outstanding remainder kept it open (paragraph 2), so a newcomer seeking ties would leave a remainder, as in B. C is the attractive trap: it invents a probationary custom of exact repayment that, under Halvik's theory, would signal the opposite of what the newcomer wants. A and E have no basis in the passage, and D borrows the idea of measures without any support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Halvik's theory to a newcomer household and predict what would likely be true of it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: exact repayment 'ended the relationship'; a small remainder kept 'perpetually outstanding' kept it open.

breakdown.analysis: The rule, as an if-then: repay exactly → relationship ends; leave a small remainder → relationship stays open. So a newcomer who wants a lasting tie with a neighbor should repay a little more or a little less than borrowed. Prephrase: to build ties, it would deliberately repay inexactly. On apply-the-theory questions, just run the theory's mechanism forward on the new case.

choices.note: No basis. Nothing suggests newcomers had to set up merchant accounts before borrowing from neighbors.

CORRECT. Under Halvik's theory, exact repayment signals a wish to end the relationship, and a small remainder keeps it open. A newcomer wanting lasting ties would repay slightly more or less than it borrowed.
The attractive trap. It invents a probation period of exact repayment. Under Halvik's theory, exact repayment would signal the opposite of what a newcomer wants: that it doesn't want to stay bound.
Unsupported. The passage never discusses different measures used with neighbors versus merchants. (That idea shows up in a later question as a challenge to Halvik, not as part of her theory.)
No basis. Labor appears in the Brenn example as one form of repayment, not as a precondition for borrowing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Halvik’s theory mentioned in the first sentence of the second paragraph?
choices: Households in a neighboring valley during the same period kept accounts with their neighbors that nearly always balanced exactly.
The Orlen ledgers rarely record the purposes for which grain or tools were borrowed.
Several of the quarrels recorded in Orlen parish registers involved families whose accounts with each other remained open afterward.
Households that kept ledgers in the Orlen Valley tended to be somewhat wealthier than households that did not.

The remainders in accounts between Orlen neighbors closely match the discrepancies produced by converting among the several inconsistent local grain measures then in use, none of which was used in dealings with outside merchants.
questions.explanation: Halvik claims the remainders were deliberate; E supplies a non-deliberate cause that explains both their small size and the contrast with exactly closed merchant accounts, undercutting her strongest evidence. C is the most tempting trap, but Halvik never claims that every quarrel closed an account, only that exact closings frequently coincided with disputes, so open accounts surviving some quarrels barely touches the theory. A concerns a different community, whose customs could differ, and B and D are irrelevant to why the remainders existed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Weaken Halvik's theory that the imbalances were deliberate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (the theory) and paragraph 3 (her evidence: exact merchant accounts, small and alternating remainders, disputes when accounts closed exactly).

breakdown.analysis: Halvik's claim is about intent: the remainders were on purpose. The best weakener gives an innocent, non-deliberate cause that also explains her key evidence. Her strongest evidence is the contrast: households could balance merchant accounts exactly, so the imbalances with neighbors must have been chosen. If something about neighbor dealings, and not merchant dealings, mechanically produces small discrepancies, that contrast loses its force. Prephrase: an accidental source of small remainders that applies only to neighbor accounts. It's like assuming a friend always leaves a dollar short on purpose, then learning the vending machine only takes quarters.

choices.note: A different community. Neighbors in another valley could have different customs, so this barely touches Halvik's claim about Orlen.
Irrelevant. Why grain or tools were borrowed doesn't bear on why repayments were inexact.

The most tempting trap. Halvik doesn't claim every quarrel closed an account, only that exact closings often coincided with disputes. Some accounts staying open after a quarrel barely hurts the theory.
Irrelevant. The wealth of ledger-keeping households doesn't explain the remainders.

CORRECT. It offers an accidental cause: converting between inconsistent local measures would produce small discrepancies. And because those measures weren't used with merchants, it also explains why merchant accounts balanced exactly. That takes away Halvik's best evidence that the remainders were deliberate.

questions.stem: The passage cites each of the following as evidence supporting Halvik’s theory EXCEPT:
choices: testimony from present-day residents of the valley describing the custom of leaving debts unsettled
the exactness with which accounts with outside merchants were closed
the small size of the remainders carried forward in accounts between neighbors
the tendency of the direction of the imbalance between two households to alternate
the coincidence of exactly closed accounts between neighbors with disputes or departures
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists the evidence: precise merchant accounts (B), small remainders (C) and alternating imbalances (D), and parish records linking exact closings to disputes or departures (E). Nothing in the passage mentions present-day testimony, so A is the exception. E can look unfamiliar because it paraphrases the 'Finally' sentence, but it is stated there.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: EXCEPT question: four choices are cited as evidence for Halvik's theory. Find the one that isn't.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, which lists her evidence: precise merchant accounts; small remainders; alternating direction; exact closings coinciding with disputes or departures.

breakdown.analysis: Make a checklist from paragraph 3: (1) merchant accounts closed exactly, (2) remainders small, (3) imbalance direction alternated, (4) exact closings coincided with disputes, lawsuits, or departures. Cross off each choice that matches. The one left over is the answer. On EXCEPT questions, a list in the passage is your best friend.

choices.note: CORRECT. Nothing in the passage mentions present-day residents. All of Halvik's evidence is historical: ledgers and parish records.
Cited: merchant accounts 'were closed to the last measure.'
Cited: remainders 'were small, typically less than a tenth of the original loan.'
Cited: 'the direction of the imbalance tended to alternate.'
Cited, in paraphrase: the 'Finally' sentence says parish records frequently note a dispute, lawsuit, or departure when neighbor accounts closed exactly.

questions.stem: The author discusses the ledger of the Brenn household primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that Orlen households valued labor more highly than grain
illustrate the kind of arithmetic error that early commentators attributed to Orlen bookkeepers
suggest that Halvik's theory applies more clearly to some kinds of loans than to others
show in a single case how alternating imbalances were sustained over many years and how such an account came to be closed
establish that quarrels over boundaries were the most common reason that accounts between neighbors were closed
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by saying the Brenn ledger 'illustrates the mechanism,' then traces the alternating imbalance for thirty-one years and its closing in the year of a quarrel, which is D. A seizes on one detail (labor valued at slightly more than a bushel) that serves only to show the imbalance flipping. E overgeneralizes from a single case, and B is the commentators' interpretation the example is meant to replace.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: why does the author walk through the Brenn household's ledger?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence: 'The ledger of the Brenn household illustrates the mechanism.' Then the thirty-one years of alternation and the 1843 closing.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph tells you its purpose in its first sentence: it 'illustrates the mechanism.' Then it shows the mechanism step by step: rye lent, a bushel over returned, labor worth slightly more than a bushel, back and forth for thirty-one years, closed in the year of a boundary quarrel. Prephrase: a single concrete example of how the alternating imbalance worked over time and how the account ended. If a paragraph announces its own job, believe it.

choices.note: Seizes on a detail. The labor being worth slightly more than a bushel just shows the balance flipping. It's not a point about valuing labor over grain.
Backwards. The example shows deliberate alternation, which is the explanation meant to replace the 'arithmetic error' reading.
No comparison of loan types. Rye and labor both appear in the same account, and both fit the theory.
CORRECT. 'Illustrates the mechanism': the Brenn-Tamm account shows the imbalance alternating for thirty-one years and finally being closed in the year of a quarrel.
Overgeneralizes from one case. A single boundary quarrel doesn't show that boundary quarrels were the most common reason accounts closed.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: How many weeks do slate pearlmussel glochidia remain encapsulated on a Halder herring before dropping off?
Why did improvements in water quality above the Ostrow Dam fail to halt the decline of the slate pearlmussel there?
Which fish species other than the Halder herring did Kovač test in the laboratory?
How much did the fish lift at the Ostrow Dam cost to build and operate?
Why do slate pearlmussels live longer than most other freshwater mussels?
questions.explanation: The passage explains that the dam ended the herring runs on which glochidia depend, so the upstream population could not reproduce whatever the water quality (paragraph 2), answering B. A is the tempting trap, but the passage says only 'several weeks,' not a specific number. C, D, and E concern information the passage never gives; it says adults live long but not why, or how that compares with other mussels.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage gives enough information to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (water quality met standards, mussels kept declining) and paragraph 2 (the dam ended the herring runs the glochidia need).

breakdown.analysis: Go through the questions and ask whether the passage actually gives the answer, not just touches the topic. The big story of the passage answers one question cleanly: why didn't cleaner water save the mussels above the dam? Because the dam blocked the herring, the only host the larvae can use, so the population couldn't reproduce no matter how clean the water got. Watch for questions that need a specific number or fact the passage only hints at.

choices.note: The tempting trap. The passage says 'several weeks,' not a specific number. 'How many weeks?' needs an exact answer the passage doesn't give.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2 explains it: glochidia transform only on Halder herring, the dam ended the herring runs, so the upstream population couldn't reproduce however clean the water was.
The passage says Kovač tested 'a dozen fish species' but never names the others.
Cost never comes up. We only learn the lift began operating in 2008.
The passage says adults can live for most of a century but never says why, or how that compares with other mussels.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the conclusions Kovač drew in 1994 (second paragraph)?
choices: Adult slate pearlmussels upstream of the dam grow more slowly than those downstream, so that their growth rings are harder to count.
Glochidia of several other mussel species in the Halder River transform successfully on many different fish species.
Halder herring tolerate polluted water better than most other fish species in the river do.
Juvenile mussels of many species are more sensitive to fine sediment than biologists believed in 1994.
In a tributary that joins the Halder above the dam and whose bed has remained free of fine sediment, the slate pearlmussels are likewise nearly all more than sixty years old.
questions.explanation: Kovač's critics proposed sediment above the dam as an alternative explanation for the missing age classes (paragraph 3); E shows the same age gap where there is no sediment but herring are still blocked, ruling out that alternative. D strengthens the critics rather than Kovač, and A casts doubt on her aging method. B concerns other species, and C is irrelevant to whether the herring's absence prevents reproduction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Strengthen Kovač's 1994 conclusions: that the upstream population stopped reproducing because the dam blocked the herring.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (her evidence: lab host tests and the age gap above the dam) and paragraph 3 (the critics' alternative: sediment above the dam killing juveniles).

breakdown.analysis: The main rival explanation for the missing young mussels is sediment: maybe juveniles were produced but couldn't survive in the silty bed above the dam. To strengthen Kovač, find a case that keeps her cause (no herring) and removes the rival cause (no sediment). If the age gap is still there, sediment can't be the explanation. Prephrase: same missing age classes in a place above the dam with no sediment. Strengthening often means ruling out the other side's alternative.

choices.note: Hurts Kovač. If upstream growth rings are harder to count, her aging method, and so her age gap, becomes less reliable.
Other species. How other mussels' glochidia behave doesn't tell us about the slate pearlmussel's need for herring.
Irrelevant. Herring pollution tolerance doesn't bear on whether their absence stopped mussel reproduction above the dam.
Strengthens the critics, not Kovač. If juveniles are more sensitive to sediment, the sediment explanation looks better.

CORRECT. A tributary above the dam (herring still blocked) with no fine sediment still has almost only 60+-year-old mussels. Sediment can't explain that gap, which leaves the missing host as the cause.

questions.stem: The information yielded by which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether the critics described in the third paragraph were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive?
choices: exposing slate pearlmussel glochidia in the laboratory to additional fish species found above the dam
counting the growth rings of slate pearlmussels collected from several sites below the dam
placing juvenile pearlmussels raised on herring in a hatchery into cages on the riverbed above the dam and monitoring their survival
comparing the number of glochidia released by female pearlmussels above the dam with the number released by females below it
measuring concentrations of industrial pollutants in the water above the dam during the herring's former spawning season
questions.explanation: The sediment critics claimed juveniles could not survive above the dam even if produced; C supplies juveniles directly and tests their survival in that riverbed, isolating survival from production. A is the strongest trap, but it tests the other objection (whether hosts in the wild differ from those in tanks), not the sediment claim. D measures larval output, which bears on production rather than juvenile survival, and B and E do not involve the upstream riverbed's effect on juveniles.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the experiment that would best test the critics' claim that juveniles were missing because they couldn't survive above the dam, not because none were produced.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence: the missing age classes 'might reflect where juveniles could survive rather than whether they were being produced.'

breakdown.analysis: The critics separate two questions: production (are juveniles being made?) and survival (can they live in that riverbed?). A good test controls production and measures survival. So put juveniles that definitely exist into the upstream riverbed and see if they live. Prephrase: put healthy juveniles in the upstream riverbed and track them. To test a cause, isolate it.

choices.note: The strongest trap. It tests the other objection: whether wild hosts differ from tank hosts. That's about production, not where juveniles can survive.
Below the dam is the wrong place. The question is whether the upstream riverbed lets juveniles survive.

CORRECT. Juveniles raised on herring are supplied directly, so production is taken out of the question, and then caged on the upstream bed. If they survive, the sediment claim fails; if they die, it gains support.
Measures larval output, which bears on production. The critics' claim is about juvenile survival.
Water pollution isn't the critics' point, and the passage says water quality already met standards. It doesn't test survival in the riverbed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Before Kovač's work, the decline of the slate pearlmussel above the Ostrow Dam had been attributed mainly to the condition of the river's water and bed.
Kovač believed that the water-quality measures begun in 1978 had harmed the slate pearlmussel.
Adult slate pearlmussels are more sensitive to fine sediment than juveniles are.
Halder herring no longer spawn anywhere in the Halder River.
The fish lift at the Ostrow Dam was built in direct response to Kovač's laboratory findings.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the decline was attributed to industrial pollution and agricultural sediment, which is the condition of the water and the bed, so A is supported. B is too strong: Kovač wanted funds redirected, not because the measures did harm but because they did not address the problem. C reverses the passage's claim about juveniles, D goes beyond it (the herring may still spawn below the dam), and E asserts a causal link the passage never draws, since the lift came fourteen years later after resistance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage most strongly supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1: 'the decline was attributed to the industrial pollution and agricultural sediment that had degraded much of the river.'

breakdown.analysis: On most-strongly-supported questions, the right answer is usually a modest restatement of something the passage says. Paragraph 1 says the decline was blamed on pollution (water) and sediment (bed) before Kovač came along in 1994. Prephrase: before Kovač, people blamed the water and the riverbed. Wrong answers will add a cause, flip a comparison, or go beyond the facts.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 1 says the decline 'was attributed to the industrial pollution and agricultural sediment' that had degraded the river. Pollution is the water's condition; sediment is the bed's. Kovač's theory came later, in 1994.
Too strong. Kovač wanted funds redirected because the cleanup didn't address the real problem, not because it caused harm.
Reversed. The passage says juveniles are more sensitive to sediment than adults.
Goes too far. The dam ended the runs upstream. The herring may still spawn below the dam, and after 2008 they're caught upstream again.
Unsupported causal link. The lift opened in 2008, fourteen years after Kovač's proposal met resistance. The passage never says it was built because of her lab work.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the surveys of the 1970s mentioned in the first paragraph?
choices: They overstated the extent of the decline, since many old mussels above the dam were still alive.
Their findings were inconsistent with the view that pollution was responsible for the decline.
They should have led biologists to examine the mussel's life cycle rather than the river's water quality.
The decline they recorded would not by itself have revealed that the population above the dam had ceased to reproduce.
They counted mussels below the dam as well as above it, which obscured the difference between the two populations.
questions.explanation: The surveys recorded falling numbers; Kovač's insight required aging the mussels, since a population of long-lived adults that has stopped reproducing appears 'merely diminished' (paragraph 2) and 'can conceal a failure of reproduction' (paragraph 4), which supports D. B is the most tempting trap, but a decline in numbers is perfectly consistent with a pollution explanation, which is why it was accepted.
