C imports a normative judgment the author never makes about the surveys, and A and E lack support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer something about the 1970s surveys from what the passage says later.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the surveys found fewer mussels each decade), paragraph 2 ('reproductively dead for decades while appearing merely diminished'), and paragraph 4 ('a population of long-lived adults can conceal a failure of reproduction').

breakdown.analysis: The 1970s surveys counted mussels and found fewer each decade. But Kovač's insight came from aging the mussels, not counting them. A population of long-lived adults that has stopped reproducing just looks smaller. So a count alone wouldn't reveal that reproduction had stopped. Prephrase: the decline in numbers wouldn't, on its own, show that reproduction had stopped. It's like counting a town's population: if it's shrinking slowly, you can't tell from the total that no babies have been born in decades. You'd need ages.

choices.note: No support. The surveys found fewer mussels each decade; nothing suggests they miscounted or overstated the drop.
The most tempting trap. A decline in numbers fits a pollution story perfectly well; that's why the pollution explanation was accepted.
A judgment the author never makes. The passage doesn't say the surveyors should have looked at the life cycle.

CORRECT. A reproductively dead population of long-lived adults appears 'merely diminished' and 'can conceal a failure of reproduction.' Counting the decline couldn't show that reproduction had stopped. It took aging the shells.
No support. The passage says the surveys were 'upstream of the Ostrow Dam' and never says they mixed in downstream counts.

questions.stem: The author mentions that recruitment was markedly lower in the siltiest reaches (middle of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the fish lift has failed to restore reproduction in most of the river above the dam
acknowledge that one objection to Kovač's account identified a genuine factor even though it did not explain the absence of young mussels
show that Kovač's critics were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive
argue that funding for water-quality measures above the dam should be restored
cast doubt on Kovač's laboratory findings about which fish could serve as hosts
questions.explanation: The sentence concedes that the sediment critics 'had identified a real, though secondary, constraint,' after the passage has shown juveniles appearing even where sediment had not changed; that is B. C is the trap: it takes the concession too far, since recruitment resumed once herring returned, showing that host absence, not sediment, explained the missing age classes. A exaggerates 'lower' into failure, and D and E are not suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: why does the author mention that recruitment was markedly lower in the siltiest reaches?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: juveniles returned 'including in reaches where sediment had not measurably changed,' then 'Recruitment was nonetheless markedly lower in the siltiest reaches, suggesting that Kovač's critics had identified a real, though secondary, constraint.'

breakdown.analysis: First, the passage shows Kovač was right: once herring returned, juveniles appeared even where sediment hadn't changed. Then it gives the critics their due: sediment still lowers recruitment, a 'real, though secondary, constraint.' Prephrase: to concede that the sediment objection was partly right, even though it didn't explain the missing juveniles. Words like 'nonetheless' and 'though secondary' signal a concession, not a reversal.

choices.note: Exaggerates 'lower' into failure. Juveniles came back above the dam; recruitment was just lower in the siltiest spots.

CORRECT. The author concedes the critics found 'a real, though secondary, constraint.' Sediment matters, but since juveniles appeared once herring returned, even where sediment was unchanged, it wasn't what caused the missing age classes.

The trap. It takes the concession too far. Juveniles reappeared once the herring came back, so the missing age classes were about the host, not where juveniles could survive. Sediment is only 'secondary.'
Not suggested. The passage makes no funding recommendation here, and water-quality funding isn't the same as sediment.
Not suggested. The herring results actually confirm her lab findings: herring upstream carried glochidia and juveniles followed.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Our league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game. The rule's supporters say it will reduce arm injuries, and that is a worthy aim. But most arm injuries among our players occur during off-season travel tournaments, which the league does not govern. So a pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the coach's argument?
choices: Reducing arm injuries among youth pitchers is a worthy aim.
Most arm injuries among the league's players occur during off-season travel tournaments.
The league should not adopt the proposed forty-pitch limit for youth pitchers.
A pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
The league should begin to govern off-season travel tournaments.
questions.explanation: The coach's point is the opening claim that the league should not adopt the pitch limit; everything else supports it, so C is correct. D is the tempting trap: it is itself supported by the claim about travel tournaments, but it is offered as the reason for rejecting the rule, making it an intermediate conclusion. A is a concession and E is never proposed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The league should not adopt the forty-pitch limit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reducing arm injuries is worthy (concession); but most arm injuries happen in off-season travel tournaments the league doesn't govern; so a league pitch limit would do little to protect arms.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion comes first here, which is common. The opening sentence is the point. The "So" sentence at the end looks like a conclusion, but ask why the coach says it: to explain why the league shouldn't adopt the rule. That makes it an intermediate step. Lesson: "so" doesn't always mark the main conclusion; check what supports what.

choices.note: A concession. The coach grants that the aim is worthy before arguing against the rule. Not the point being proved.
A premise. It's the evidence that the pitch limit wouldn't help much.
CORRECT. The opening claim. Everything else (the travel tournaments, the little protection the rule would give) is there to support it.
The trap. It's supported by the tournament fact, so it is a conclusion, but it's offered as the reason not to adopt the rule. Intermediate, not main.
The coach never proposes this. Mentioning that the league doesn't govern tournaments isn't the same as saying it should.

questions.stimulus: Owner of Kessel's Bakery: In March we began setting out free samples of our pastries on the counter, and our pastry sales in March were 15 percent higher than in February. So offering free samples is an effective way to increase our pastry sales, and we should keep doing it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that something other than the samples accounts for the rise in March sales
presumes that customers who tried a sample bought only the kind of pastry they sampled
fails to establish that the rise in pastry sales increased the bakery's overall profits
takes for granted that what works for one bakery will work for every bakery
treats the owner's own taste in pastries as representative of the customers' tastes
questions.explanation: The owner infers that the samples caused the March increase merely because the increase followed them; a seasonal shift or some other change could explain it, so A is correct. C is tempting, but the conclusion is only about increasing pastry sales, not profits. The argument never generalizes beyond this bakery (D) or relies on the owner's taste (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Free samples are an effective way to increase pastry sales, and the bakery should keep offering them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Samples started in March; March pastry sales were 15% higher than February's.

breakdown.analysis: Something happened, then sales went up, so the something caused it. That's the "after this, therefore because of this" flaw. February is short and cold; March might just be busier. Maybe there was a holiday, a new menu item, or a street fair. It's like saying your new umbrella made it stop raining because the rain stopped after you bought it. Prephrase: the owner ignores other reasons for the March jump.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only evidence is that sales rose after samples started. Seasonal traffic or any other change could explain it, and the owner never rules those out.
The owner doesn't assume anything about which pastries sample-tasters bought. The conclusion is about total pastry sales.
choices.example: Example of flaw: People who tried our free cinnamon roll sample must have bought cinnamon rolls, so samples only boost the sampled item.

choices.note: Tempting, but the conclusion is about pastry sales, not profits. The owner doesn't need to show anything about profit to claim sales went up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our sales rose 20% after the discount, so the discount must have made us more money.

choices.note: The owner talks only about this bakery. No generalization to every bakery.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Free samples boosted sales at our bakery, so every bakery in the country should offer them.

choices.note: The owner's own taste never comes up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: I love the almond croissant, so it should be our best seller.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: This summer the tomato plants in my plot, which I mulched with straw, produced far fewer split fruits than the unmulched tomato plants in my neighbor's plot. Tomatoes split when soil moisture swings sharply, and straw mulch keeps soil moisture steady. So mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gardener's argument?
choices: Straw mulch also suppresses weeds that compete with tomato plants for nutrients.
Some tomato varieties are much more prone to splitting than others are.
The gardener's neighbor harvested more tomatoes in total this summer than the gardener did.
The few tomato plants in the gardener's own plot that were left unmulched split about as often as the neighbor's plants did.
Tomato splitting tends to be more common in years with heavy late-summer rain.
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two different plots, so some difference other than mulch (variety, watering, soil) could explain the result. D shows that unmulched plants in the gardener's own plot split as often as the neighbor's, isolating mulch as the relevant difference. B is tempting but only raises a possible alternative cause without saying the plots differed in variety, so it if anything weakens; E affects both plots alike.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The gardener's straw-mulched plants split far less than the neighbor's unmulched plants; tomatoes split when soil moisture swings sharply; straw keeps soil moisture steady.

breakdown.analysis: Two different plots, one difference named: mulch. But the plots could differ in variety, watering, soil, or sun. To strengthen, isolate the mulch. Best fix: compare mulched and unmulched plants in the same plot. If the gardener's own unmulched plants split like the neighbor's, the plot isn't the difference; the mulch is.

choices.note: Another benefit of straw (weeds), but weeds aren't connected to splitting. Doesn't help the argument.
Tempting, but it only raises the possibility that variety matters. It doesn't say the plots grew different varieties. If anything it hints at a rival cause, which weakens.
Total harvest says nothing about splitting rates. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. Same plot, same soil, same gardener, same watering, but unmulched plants split like the neighbor's. That isolates mulch as the factor that makes the difference.
Heavy rain would affect both plots alike. A factor shared by both sides can't explain the gap or strengthen the explanation.

questions.stimulus: Striped grunters, a reef fish found off Varrow Island, feed mostly at night, when they are most active. Yet divers who survey the reef during the day count far more striped grunters than divers who survey it at night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why divers count more striped grunters by day than by night?
choices: Striped grunters are preyed upon by several species of eels that hunt at night.
At night striped grunters scatter singly across distant seagrass beds to feed, but by day they rest in large schools directly over the reef.
Divers surveying the reef at night carry powerful lights that make fish visible at a distance.
The striped grunter is among the most abundant fish species on the reef.
Many other fish species found near Varrow Island also feed mostly at night.
questions.explanation: One would expect a fish active at night to be easier to find at night. B explains the pattern: by day the grunters gather in plain view over the reef that divers survey, while at night they disperse away from it. C deepens the puzzle, and A does not explain why the fish would be seen more often by day.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Striped grunters are most active and feed at night, but divers count far more of them during the day than at night.

breakdown.analysis: You'd expect a night-active fish to be easier to spot at night. But the divers survey the reef. If the fish leave the reef to feed at night and gather over it by day, then daytime surveys of the reef would naturally find more. It's like counting office workers at the office: you'll count more at 2 p.m. than at 2 a.m., even if they're more "active" at a nightclub. Prephrase: the fish aren't on the reef at night.

choices.note: Night predators might make grunters hide at night, but this doesn't say they do. It doesn't explain why divers see more of them by day.
CORRECT. At night they scatter to distant seagrass beds; by day they school right over the reef. Divers surveying the reef will see far more by day. Both facts are now true at once.
Powerful lights should make night counts higher. This makes the puzzle worse.
Abundance applies day and night equally. Doesn't explain a day-night difference.
Other fish feeding at night doesn't explain anything about grunter counts.

questions.stimulus: Health official: The rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma in Tarrow County is twice that in neighboring Ellis County. The air in Tarrow contains far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's air does, mostly from Tarrow's freight yards. Therefore, reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow would lower its rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the health official's argument?
choices: Diesel exhaust is the primary cause of childhood asthma in Tarrow County.
Ellis County has no freight yards or other major sources of diesel exhaust.
Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow County would also lower the rate of respiratory illness among adults there.
Children in Tarrow County with asthma attacks are more likely than those in Ellis County to be taken to a hospital.
Exposure to diesel exhaust can contribute to children's asthma becoming severe enough to require hospitalization.
questions.explanation: If diesel exhaust could not worsen children's asthma to the point of hospitalization, cutting it would do nothing to the hospitalization rate, so the argument requires E. A is the tempting trap but is too strong: exhaust need only be one contributing factor, not the primary cause of asthma. B is not needed (Ellis need only have less exhaust), and D would weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow would lower its childhood asthma hospitalization rate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tarrow's childhood asthma hospitalization rate is twice Ellis's; Tarrow's air has far more diesel exhaust, mostly from freight yards.

breakdown.analysis: The official predicts that cutting exhaust would cut hospitalizations. That only works if exhaust can actually make kids' asthma bad enough to land them in the hospital. If exhaust can't do that, cutting it changes nothing. Keep it minimal: exhaust just has to be able to contribute, not be the main cause. Use the negation test.

choices.note: Too strong. Exhaust only needs to be one contributor to hospitalizations. Negated (exhaust isn't the primary cause), cutting it could still reduce hospitalizations. Argument survives.
choices.negation: Diesel exhaust is not the primary cause of childhood asthma in Tarrow County.

choices.note: Not needed. Ellis just needs less exhaust than Tarrow, which we're told. Negated (Ellis has some freight yards), the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Ellis County has freight yards or other major sources of diesel exhaust.

choices.note: Adults are irrelevant. The argument is about childhood asthma. Negated, nothing changes.
choices.negation: Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow County would not lower the rate of respiratory illness among adults there.

choices.note: This weakens. If Tarrow kids are just more likely to be taken to the hospital, the higher rate could come from that, not the air. Negating it actually helps the argument, so it isn't required.
choices.negation: Children in Tarrow County with asthma attacks are not more likely than those in Ellis County to be taken to a hospital.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, diesel exhaust cannot contribute to hospital-level asthma in kids. Then reducing it can't lower hospitalizations, and the conclusion dies. Required.
choices.negation: Exposure to diesel exhaust cannot contribute to children's asthma becoming severe enough to require hospitalization.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The Marlton city orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works. Those works draw the largest audiences, and ticket sales are what keep the orchestra solvent.

Malik: Ticket sales certainly matter. But an orchestra that plays only familiar works will gradually lose younger listeners, who are its future audience. The orchestra should give a substantial share of its programs to new compositions.
questions.stem: Rosa and Malik disagree over whether
choices: ticket sales are important to the orchestra's financial health
established classical works draw larger audiences than new compositions do
the orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works
younger listeners prefer new compositions to established classical works
the orchestra is currently in financial difficulty
questions.explanation: Rosa says nearly all programs should be established works; Malik says a substantial share should be new compositions, which rules out 'nearly all,' so they disagree about C. Malik concedes that ticket sales matter (A) and never disputes that classics draw larger audiences (B). Rosa says nothing about younger listeners' preferences (D), and neither says the orchestra is in difficulty (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rosa: Nearly all programs should be established classical works, because they draw the biggest audiences and ticket sales keep the orchestra solvent.; Malik: Ticket sales matter, but playing only familiar works loses younger listeners; a substantial share of programs should be new compositions.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Rosa says yes to "nearly all classics." Malik says a substantial share should be new music, which means "nearly all classics" is a no. Everything else is either conceded by one side or mentioned by only one speaker. Lesson: watch for concessions like "certainly matter"; they take an answer off the table.

choices.note: They agree. Malik says "Ticket sales certainly matter."
Rosa says it; Malik never disputes it. His worry is the future audience, not today's crowd sizes. No clear disagreement.
CORRECT. Rosa: yes, nearly all programs should be classics. Malik: a substantial share should be new compositions, so no. A direct yes/no split.
Only Malik touches younger listeners, and even he only says they'll be lost with all-familiar programs. Rosa has no view on this.
Neither says the orchestra is in trouble. Rosa says ticket sales keep it solvent, which suggests it's fine.

questions.stimulus: Transit planner: Since the city raised the fare on Route 9 buses from $1.50 to $2.00 last year, Route 9 ridership has fallen by a third. To win back those riders, we should return the fare to $1.50.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit planner's argument?
choices: Shortly after the fare increase, a new light-rail line opened along most of Route 9's path, and many former Route 9 riders now use it.
Ridership on several of the city's other bus routes also fell after the fare increase.
Even at $2.00, the Route 9 fare is lower than bus fares in most comparable cities.
Returning the fare to $1.50 would reduce the transit system's revenue per rider.
Some Route 9 riders have complained about crowded buses during rush hour.
questions.explanation: The planner assumes the fare increase drove riders away, so lowering the fare would bring them back. A offers another cause of the decline, a competing rail line, which a fare cut would not undo. B tends to support the fare explanation, and C and D are about comparisons and revenue rather than about why riders left.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: To win back lost riders, the city should return the Route 9 fare to $1.50.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the fare rose from $1.50 to $2.00, Route 9 ridership has fallen by a third.

breakdown.analysis: The planner assumes the fare hike drove riders away, so undoing it will bring them back. Weaken by giving another cause for the drop that a fare cut wouldn't fix. It's like a store raising prices the same month a competitor opens next door and blaming only the prices when customers leave.

choices.note: CORRECT. A new light-rail line along most of the route opened right after the hike, and many former riders use it now. That's a different reason they left, and cutting the bus fare won't pull them off the train.
If other routes also lost riders after the increase, that fits the fare explanation. If anything it supports the planner.
A comparison to other cities' fares doesn't tell us why Route 9 riders left. Riders could still find $2.00 too much compared with $1.50.
Revenue is a cost of the plan, but the planner's argument is about winning riders back. This doesn't attack whether the fare cut would work.
Crowding complaints from "some" riders don't explain a one-third drop. Irrelevant, and crowded buses even suggest plenty of riders at rush hour.

questions.stimulus: In Darrow County, defendants awaiting trial who cannot afford bail remain in jail. A study of the county's criminal cases found that defendants held in jail before trial were more likely to plead guilty than were released defendants facing similar charges and comparably strong evidence. Many of the jailed defendants who pleaded guilty were sentenced to the time they had already served.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most defendants in Darrow County who plead guilty are in fact innocent.
Defendants in Darrow County who are released before trial are less likely to be convicted at trial.
Bail amounts in Darrow County are higher than those in most other counties.
In Darrow County, some defendants' decisions to plead guilty are influenced by factors other than the strength of the evidence against them.
Eliminating bail in Darrow County would cut the number of guilty pleas there roughly in half.
questions.explanation: Jailed and released defendants with comparably strong evidence pleaded guilty at different rates, so something besides the evidence, such as being jailed, affects some decisions to plead; D follows. A is the tempting overreach: the facts show pleas are influenced by detention, not that most who plead are innocent. B, C, and E introduce trials, other counties, and a specific number the facts do not address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Defendants who can't afford bail stay in jail before trial; 2) jailed defendants were more likely to plead guilty than released defendants facing similar charges and comparably strong evidence; 3) many jailed defendants who pleaded guilty got sentences equal to time already served.

breakdown.analysis: The study holds charges and evidence roughly constant and still finds jailed defendants pleading guilty more. So something other than the evidence must be pushing some of those pleas, probably jail itself (plead and walk out today). The safe answer: some pleas are influenced by factors besides the strength of the evidence. Keep it modest; don't jump to innocence or specific numbers.

choices.note: The overreach. The facts show detention affects pleas, not that most people who plead are innocent. Huge leap.
The study is about pleas, not trial outcomes. We know nothing about conviction rates at trial.
No other counties are mentioned. Unsupported comparison.
CORRECT. Similar charges, similar evidence, different plea rates depending on jail. So for some defendants, something besides the evidence is shaping the decision. "Some" keeps it safe.
"Roughly in half" is a specific number the facts never give. We don't know how big the effect is.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: Any field planted with winter rye after the harvest will lose less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would. All of the Hollis farm's fields will be planted with winter rye after this fall's harvest. So the Hollis farm will qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
questions.stem: The agronomist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only farms that plant winter rye on all of their fields qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Any farm all of whose fields will lose less soil to erosion over the winter than they otherwise would qualifies for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Every farm that qualifies for the county's soil-conservation grant loses less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would.
Most farms that plant winter rye after the harvest qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Winter rye reduces winter soil erosion more than any other crop that can be planted after the harvest.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every Hollis field will lose less soil over the winter; B makes exactly that a sufficient condition for the grant, so the conclusion follows. A is the attractive trap, but 'only' gives a necessary condition for qualifying, not a guarantee. C reverses the needed conditional, and D's 'most' cannot guarantee that this particular farm qualifies.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Hollis farm will qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Winter rye after harvest → less winter erosion than otherwise; all Hollis fields will get winter rye after this harvest.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Hollis fields get rye → each field loses less soil. Conclusion: Hollis qualifies for the grant. Missing link: all fields lose less soil → qualifies for grant. The conclusion term (grant) shows up only in the conclusion, so the right answer must bring it in as a result, not a requirement. Rye on all fields → less erosion on all fields → [assumed] → grant.

choices.note: The trap. "Only" makes rye on all fields a requirement for the grant, not a guarantee. Hollis meets the requirement, but that doesn't mean it qualifies.
CORRECT. All fields lose less soil → qualifies. The premises show every Hollis field will lose less soil, so Hollis qualifies. Airtight.
Reversed. Qualifies → less erosion. That tells us what grant winners look like, not that Hollis is one.
"Most" can't guarantee anything about Hollis in particular. It might be in the minority.
Compares rye with other crops. Doesn't say anything about the grant.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: Each of the five starters on the Harbor City basketball team was chosen for the regional all-star squad last season. So the Harbor City team must have been the best team in the region last season.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the judgment of all-star selectors who may know little about how well players work together
takes for granted that the regional all-star squad included players from every team in the region
takes for granted that players were chosen as all-stars solely for their scoring
draws a conclusion about every season from evidence about a single season
presumes that a team whose individual starters are outstanding must itself be outstanding as a team
questions.explanation: The sportswriter moves from the excellence of each starter to the excellence of the team as a whole, though a team of strong individuals can still play poorly together; E describes this. A is tempting because it mentions teamwork, but the argument's problem is not reliance on the selectors' judgment of individuals, which may be sound. The conclusion concerns only last season (D), and nothing presumes all-stars were chosen for scoring (C).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Harbor City was the best team in the region last season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All five Harbor City starters were chosen for the regional all-star squad last season.

breakdown.analysis: Part-to-whole flaw. Great parts don't guarantee a great whole. Five all-stars might not pass, defend together, or have a bench. It's like assuming a band with five brilliant soloists must be the best band; they might clash horribly. Prephrase: the argument assumes a team of outstanding individuals is an outstanding team.

choices.note: Tempting because it mentions teamwork. But the argument doesn't depend on selectors judging teamwork; they judge individuals, and that may be fine. The real problem is going from individuals to the team.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Critics who know nothing about acting chose this film's cast, so the film must be well acted.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need every team represented. It just uses the fact that Harbor City's five were all picked.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our town had three winners in the state science fair, so every town in the state must have entered.

choices.note: Nothing in the argument depends on why players were picked. Scoring never comes up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: She was named player of the year, so she must have led the league in points.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about last season. No generalization to every season.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We won the title last year, so we'll be the best team every year.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument moves from "each starter is outstanding" to "the team is outstanding." Strong parts don't guarantee a strong whole.

questions.stimulus: Dr. Imani: Some residents want the city to stop fluoridating its water because a few people have reported mild tooth discoloration. But by that standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water, since chlorine sometimes gives water an unpleasant taste. No one seriously proposes ending chlorination, which protects against waterborne disease. So mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.
questions.stem: Dr. Imani's argument proceeds by
choices: showing that the reasoning behind a proposal would, if applied consistently, support a conclusion that is clearly unacceptable
offering evidence that the reported tooth discoloration was not in fact caused by fluoridation
arguing that the benefits of fluoridation are greater than the benefits of chlorination
questioning the motives of the residents who reported tooth discoloration
citing expert opinion to establish that fluoridation poses no health risks
questions.explanation: Dr. Imani argues that the residents' standard (a minor side effect justifies ending a treatment) would also require ending chlorination, an absurd result, so A is correct. B is tempting because it seems a natural rebuttal, but Dr. Imani never disputes that fluoridation caused the discoloration. She does not rank the benefits of the two treatments (C), attack motives (D), or cite experts (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mild tooth discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By the residents' standard (a minor side effect justifies ending a treatment), the city would also have to end chlorination, which sometimes tastes bad; no one seriously proposes that, since chlorine prevents waterborne disease.

breakdown.analysis: Dr. Imani doesn't argue directly about fluoride. She takes the residents' reasoning and shows where it leads if you apply it everywhere: you'd have to stop chlorinating, which is absurd. So the reasoning must be bad. That's a reductio-style analogy. Like saying "If 'it sometimes causes headaches' is enough to ban coffee, then we'd have to ban sunlight too."

choices.note: CORRECT. She applies the residents' standard to chlorination and gets an obviously unacceptable result. That's exactly showing that the reasoning, applied consistently, leads somewhere absurd.
Tempting, because it's a natural rebuttal. But she never questions whether fluoride caused the discoloration. She accepts it and argues it's not enough.
choices.example: Example of method: Residents blame the new factory for the stained laundry, but the stains started months before the factory opened.

choices.note: She never ranks fluoride's benefits against chlorine's. Chlorine is just the example that exposes the bad standard.
choices.example: Example of method: Fluoridation prevents far more harm than chlorination does, so it is the more important treatment to keep.

choices.note: No attack on motives. She treats the residents' complaint seriously and responds to their reasoning.
choices.example: Example of method: The residents complaining about fluoride all sell bottled water, so their concerns shouldn't be taken seriously.

choices.note: She cites no experts and never claims fluoride has zero risks. She grants a side effect exists.
choices.example: Example of method: The national dental association says fluoridation is completely safe, so the city should continue it.

questions.stimulus: Dunmore Hardware policy: An employee may approve a customer refund only if the employee has completed the store's register training. Every employee who works weekend shifts has completed register training. Jalen, a Dunmore Hardware employee, has not completed register training.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every Dunmore Hardware employee who has completed register training may approve refunds.
Every Dunmore Hardware employee who may approve refunds works weekend shifts.
Jalen does not work weekend shifts at Dunmore Hardware.
Some Dunmore Hardware employees who have not completed register training work weekend shifts.
Jalen will complete register training before he is assigned any weekend shifts.
questions.explanation: Working weekends guarantees completed training, so by the contrapositive anyone without the training, including Jalen, does not work weekends; C must be true. A reverses the first rule, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. B does not follow, because trained employees who approve refunds might work only weekdays, and D contradicts the second rule.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Approve refunds → completed register training; 2) works weekend shifts → completed register training; 3) Jalen has not completed register training.

breakdown.analysis: Jalen lacks training. Run both contrapositives: no training → can't approve refunds, and no training → doesn't work weekends. So Jalen can't approve refunds and doesn't work weekends. Both rules point to training as a requirement; neither says training is enough for anything.

choices.note: Reverses rule 1. Training is required to approve refunds, not enough to approve them.
Doesn't follow. Refund approvers and weekend workers both have training, but that doesn't make them the same people. A weekday-only trained employee could approve refunds.
CORRECT. Weekend → trained. Contrapositive: not trained → no weekends. Jalen isn't trained, so he doesn't work weekends.
Contradicts rule 2: every weekend worker has completed training.
A prediction about the future that the rules don't support. Jalen might never get weekend shifts or training.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: Five years ago, bottom trawling was banned in Selby Bay. Since then, the number of juvenile cod counted in the bay's annual survey has tripled. Evidently, the ban has allowed the bay's cod population to recover.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the marine biologist's argument?
choices: Does bottom trawling also harm fish species other than cod?
Was the trawling ban supported by most of the bay's commercial fishing crews?
Has the cost of enforcing the ban exceeded the original estimates?
Was bottom trawling banned in Selby Bay before it was banned in other bays in the region?
Did juvenile cod counts rise by a similar amount over the same period in nearby waters where bottom trawling continued?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the ban with the rise in juvenile cod, but a regionwide trend could explain it. If counts rose just as much where trawling continued, the ban looks irrelevant; if not, the ban is better supported, so E matters. A and D are on topic but do not bear on whether the ban caused this rise, and B and C concern politics and cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The trawling ban allowed Selby Bay's cod population to recover.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Bottom trawling was banned five years ago; since then, the juvenile cod count has tripled.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causal claim. The obvious rival: maybe cod bounced back everywhere because of water temperature or a good spawning cycle. The best evaluate question compares with a control: places where trawling continued. If they also tripled, the ban looks irrelevant. If they didn't, the ban looks like the cause.

choices.note: On topic, but whether trawling hurts other species doesn't tell us whether the ban caused this cod rise.
Support from fishing crews is politics. Doesn't bear on whether cod recovered because of the ban.
Enforcement cost has nothing to do with the cod population.
Order of bans doesn't tell us whether this ban caused this rise. Neither answer changes the argument.
CORRECT. Yes, similar rise where trawling continued → something regional, the ban looks irrelevant. No → the ban is the likely difference. Either answer moves the argument a lot.

questions.stimulus: Prosecutors should offer a defendant a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea only if the defendant has no prior conviction for a violent offense and, in any case with an identifiable victim, the victim has been told of the proposed offer.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Ortiz has no prior convictions, and the victim of his theft has been told of the proposed offer. So the prosecutor should offer Ortiz a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
Hale has no prior convictions of any kind, but the owner of the shop Hale vandalized has not been told of the proposed offer. So the prosecutor should not yet offer Hale a reduced charge.
Pryce has a prior conviction for fraud, which is not a violent offense. So the prosecutor should not offer Pryce a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
Lam's offense had no identifiable victim, though Lam has a prior conviction for assault. So the prosecutor may offer Lam a reduced charge once the community has been consulted.
The victim of Reyes's burglary was told of the proposed offer and objected to it. So the prosecutor should not offer Reyes a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions, so it can justify only a conclusion that an offer should not be made when a condition fails. In B the shop owner, an identifiable victim, has not been told, so the offer should not be made yet. A is the main trap: both conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions does not show the offer should be made. E is also tempting, but the principle requires only that the victim be told, not that the victim agree, and C misapplies it because fraud is not a violent offense.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Offer reduced charge for a guilty plea → no prior violent conviction AND (if there's an identifiable victim) the victim has been told. Contrapositive: prior violent conviction OR identifiable victim not told → do not offer.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" sets up necessary conditions. So the principle never tells you to make an offer; it only tells you when you shouldn't. The right answer will show a condition failing and conclude "don't offer." Like "you can enter only if you have a ticket": having a ticket doesn't mean you must be let in, but no ticket means no entry.

choices.note: The main trap. Ortiz meets both conditions, but meeting necessary conditions doesn't mean the offer should be made. The principle can't justify "should offer."
CORRECT. There's an identifiable victim (the shop owner) who hasn't been told. A condition fails, so per the contrapositive the offer shouldn't be made, at least not yet.
Misapplies it. Fraud isn't violent, so Pryce doesn't fail the conviction condition. The principle gives no reason to deny him.
Backwards. Lam has a prior assault conviction, which is violent, so the principle says don't offer. And "once the community has been consulted" comes from nowhere.
Tempting, but the principle requires only that the victim be told, not that the victim agree. The objection isn't a condition, so the principle can't justify denying the offer.

questions.stimulus: City engineer: At the intersections where we replaced four-way stop signs with small traffic circles, collisions fell by 40 percent the following year. Drivers must slow down to get through a traffic circle, and slower speeds mean fewer collisions. So we should install traffic circles at the city's remaining four-way-stop intersections as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city engineer's argument?
choices: Traffic circles cost less to maintain than traffic signals do.
Many drivers say they find traffic circles confusing the first time they encounter them.
In the year before the conversion, the converted intersections had more collisions than any other intersections in the city.
The intersections that were converted were chosen at random from among all of the city's four-way-stop intersections.
Some of the collisions at the converted intersections in the following year involved pedestrians.
questions.explanation: The engineer generalizes from the converted intersections to the rest. If those intersections were picked at random (D), they are representative of the remaining ones, and an unusual year at specially chosen sites is less likely to explain the drop. C is the trap: it actually weakens the argument, because intersections chosen for their unusually bad record would tend to improve anyway and may differ from the rest. A compares circles with signals, which is not the alternative under discussion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should install traffic circles at its remaining four-way-stop intersections.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Converted intersections saw collisions fall 40% the next year; traffic circles force drivers to slow down, and slower speeds mean fewer collisions.

breakdown.analysis: The engineer generalizes from the converted intersections to all the rest. That works only if the converted ones are typical. If the city picked its worst intersections, they'd likely improve anyway (a bad year tends to be followed by a less bad one), and they might differ from the rest. The best strengthener shows the converted sites are representative. Random selection does exactly that.

choices.note: Compares circles with traffic signals, but the plan replaces stop signs, not signals. Wrong comparison.
Confusion on first encounter is if anything a cost of circles. Doesn't strengthen.

The trap. It sounds like proof circles helped the worst spots, but it actually weakens: the worst intersections would tend to improve anyway, and they aren't like the rest of the city's intersections.

CORRECT. Randomly chosen intersections are representative of the rest, and random choice rules out "they picked the worst spots, which bounced back on their own." The 40% drop now tells us more about what circles would do elsewhere.
Pedestrian collisions are part of the remaining 60%. That says nothing about whether circles caused the drop or would work elsewhere.

questions.stimulus: After farmers in the Kell Valley switched from flooding their orchards to drip irrigation, they used about 30 percent less water per acre. Yet the total amount of water drawn from the valley's aquifer for agriculture rose in the years after drip irrigation became widespread.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why agricultural water use in the Kell Valley rose?
choices: Drip irrigation made it profitable to grow orchards on hilly land that could not be flood-irrigated, so many farmers greatly expanded their irrigated acreage.
Drip irrigation systems cost more to install than flood irrigation systems do.
A few farmers in the valley continued to flood their orchards after drip irrigation became widespread.
The amount of water drawn from the aquifer by households in the valley also rose during those years.
Drip irrigation reduces the amount of irrigation water lost to evaporation.
questions.explanation: Less water per acre can still mean more water in total if many more acres are irrigated; A supplies exactly that increase in acreage. C is tempting, but holdouts who kept flooding would only limit the savings, not produce a rise above earlier levels. D concerns household rather than agricultural use, and E explains only the per-acre savings.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Drip irrigation cut water use per acre by about 30%, but total agricultural water drawn from the aquifer rose after drip irrigation spread.

breakdown.analysis: Total = per-acre use × number of acres. If per-acre use fell and the total rose, the number of acres must have gone up a lot. Quick math: 100 acres at 10 units = 1,000; after the switch, 7 units an acre on 200 acres = 1,400. Prephrase: farmers irrigated many more acres. It's like a car with better gas mileage making you drive so much more that you end up buying more gas.

choices.note: CORRECT. Drip irrigation opened up hilly land that couldn't be flooded, and farmers greatly expanded their irrigated acreage. Less water per acre times many more acres can easily mean more water overall.
Installation cost doesn't tell us anything about water use. If anything, pricier systems would slow adoption.
Tempting, but a few holdouts would just shrink the savings. They used the same water as before, so they can't push the total above earlier levels.
Household use is a different category. The puzzle is about agricultural water.
Explains the per-acre savings, which is half of the puzzle we already accept. Doesn't explain why the total went up.

questions.stimulus: Music teacher: Students who practice an instrument in many short sessions each week generally improve faster than students who practice for the same total time in a few long sessions. Yet most of my students prefer a few long sessions, because those are easier to fit into their schedules.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the music teacher's statements?
choices: Students who practice in a few long sessions each week do not improve.
Most of the teacher's students improve more slowly than the students of other music teachers.
A student's schedule is the most important factor in how quickly that student improves.
The teacher should require students to practice in short sessions.
Some of the teacher's students would probably improve faster if they practiced for the same total time in more frequent, shorter sessions.
questions.explanation: Since short sessions generally produce faster improvement at the same total time, and most of the teacher's students use long sessions, some of them would probably improve faster by switching; E is appropriately hedged. A is too strong, since long sessions only produce slower improvement. D is tempting but recommends a policy the statements never address, and B compares students with other teachers' students.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) For the same total practice time, many short sessions generally lead to faster improvement than a few long ones; 2) most of the teacher's students prefer a few long sessions because they fit schedules better.

breakdown.analysis: Put them together: short sessions generally work better, and most of these students use long ones. So some of them would probably improve faster if they switched. "Generally" and "probably" keep it honest. Watch for answers that say long sessions don't work at all, or that tell the teacher what to do.

choices.note: Too strong. Long sessions produce slower improvement, not zero improvement.
Compares with other teachers' students, who are never mentioned. Unsupported.
"Most important factor" goes way beyond the facts. Schedules explain why students choose long sessions; they aren't ranked against anything else.
Tempting, but it's a policy recommendation. The statements describe what works and what students prefer; they never say what the teacher should require.
CORRECT. Short sessions generally beat long ones at the same total time, and most of these students use long ones, so some of them would probably improve faster by switching. Properly hedged.

questions.stimulus: Every swimmer on the Ridgefield club who breaks a club record during the season is invited to the regional training camp. Odile, a Ridgefield swimmer, was invited to the regional training camp this year. So Odile must have broken a club record this season.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Every chef who trains at the Marlow Institute learns to make stock from scratch. Petra did not train at the Marlow Institute, so she must not have learned to make stock from scratch.
Every apartment in the Elgin Building has a balcony. Dev's apartment has no balcony, so it must not be in the Elgin Building.
Every customer who spends more than $100 at Fenwick's receives a discount coupon. Yusuf received a discount coupon from Fenwick's, so he must have spent more than $100 there.
Only students who pass the entrance exam are admitted to Carlow Academy. Lena was admitted to Carlow Academy, so she must have passed the entrance exam.
Most volunteers who attend the orientation stay with the program for a full year. Malik attended the orientation, so he will probably stay for a full year.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a sufficient condition (breaking a record guarantees an invitation) as if it were necessary, inferring the record from the invitation. C makes the same error, inferring big spending from the coupon, since coupons may be given for other reasons. D looks identical on the surface but is valid, because 'only' makes passing the exam necessary for admission. A commits a different error (denying the antecedent), and B and E are reasonable.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Odile must have broken a club record this season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Ridgefield swimmer who breaks a club record is invited to the regional camp; Odile was invited.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A get B; X got B; so X is A (affirming the consequent).

breakdown.analysis: Record → invitation. The argument runs it backwards: invitation → record. But people could get invited for other reasons, like a coach's pick or a fast time that isn't a record. It's like "everyone who wins the lottery is happy; Sam is happy; so Sam won the lottery." Find the answer that reverses a sufficient condition in the same way.

choices.note: Flawed, but a different flaw: denying the first part. "Didn't train at Marlow, so didn't learn stock" ignores other ways to learn. It's the negation mistake, not the reversal mistake.
Valid. All Elgin apartments have balconies; no balcony → not Elgin. That's a correct contrapositive.
CORRECT. Spend $100+ → coupon. Yusuf got a coupon, so he must have spent $100+. Same reversal: coupons could come from other promotions. Exact match.
Looks identical but is valid. "Only students who pass are admitted" makes passing necessary for admission. Admitted → passed is exactly right.
Reasonable. "Most" supports "probably," and the conclusion is hedged to match. Not flawed.

questions.stimulus: Consultant: Coffee shops in Brayton that offer free wireless internet have, on average, higher daily revenue than Brayton coffee shops that do not. So the Corner Cup, a Brayton coffee shop that does not offer wireless internet, would increase its daily revenue by offering it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultant's argument?
choices: Offering free wireless internet costs a coffee shop relatively little each month.
Most of the Brayton shops that now offer free wireless internet already had higher daily revenue than other Brayton shops before they began offering it.
Several regular customers of the Corner Cup have asked its owner to offer wireless internet.
Coffee shops in nearby towns that offer free wireless internet also tend to have higher revenue than those that do not.
Some Brayton coffee shops that offer free wireless internet have lower daily revenue than the Corner Cup does.
questions.explanation: The consultant infers from a correlation that wireless internet raises revenue. B shows the revenue gap existed before the service was offered, suggesting that busier shops tend to adopt wireless rather than wireless making shops busier. E is the trap: a comparison of averages allows some wireless shops to earn less, so E does nothing to undercut the claim that wireless raises revenue. C and D tend to support the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Corner Cup would increase its daily revenue by offering free wireless internet.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brayton coffee shops with free wireless have higher average daily revenue than those without.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. Wireless shops earn more, so wireless causes higher revenue. But maybe the arrow runs the other way: busy, successful shops are the ones that can afford and bother to add wireless. If the revenue gap existed before wireless, wireless didn't create it. Like noticing that people with expensive watches are rich and concluding that buying a watch makes you rich.

choices.note: Low cost makes adding wireless a better idea, if anything. Doesn't attack whether it raises revenue.
CORRECT. The wireless shops were already earning more before they offered it. So the gap isn't from wireless; it looks like successful shops adopt wireless, not that wireless makes shops successful.
Customers asking for wireless suggests demand, which supports the plan.
Same pattern in other towns repeats the correlation. If anything it supports the argument, though it shares the same weakness.
The trap. The consultant talks about averages, and an average leaves room for some wireless shops to earn less. Doesn't touch the claim that wireless raises revenue.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Sea otters, absent from Calder Sound for decades, returned there twelve years ago. Otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. Since the otters' return, the sound's kelp forests have more than doubled in area. Thus, the otters' return is probably the main reason for the expansion of the kelp forests.
questions.stem: The ecologist's argument requires assuming which one of the following?
choices: Sea otters eat more sea urchins than any other predator in Calder Sound does.
Water temperatures in Calder Sound have not changed during the past twelve years.
Expanded kelp forests provide sea otters with shelter from their own predators.
Before the otters returned, sea urchins in Calder Sound were numerous enough to limit the growth of its kelp forests.
Sea urchins in Calder Sound eat no food other than kelp.
questions.explanation: The argument's mechanism is that otters reduce urchins, and fewer urchins let kelp grow. If urchins were too few before the otters returned to hold the kelp back (the negation of D), removing some of them could not explain the expansion. B is tempting, but a temperature change need not have affected kelp, so the argument does not require that temperatures stayed constant. A and E are stronger than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The otters' return is probably the main reason the kelp forests expanded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Otters returned twelve years ago; otters eat urchins; urchins graze kelp; since the return, kelp area has more than doubled.

breakdown.analysis: The mechanism: otters eat urchins → fewer urchins → more kelp. That only works if urchins were actually holding the kelp back before. If there were only a few urchins nibbling around the edges, removing some wouldn't free up much kelp. Like saying you got more sleep because the neighbor's dog left, when the dog never barked at night anyway. Use the negation test.

choices.note: Too strong. Otters don't need to be the top urchin eater, just eat enough to make a difference. Negated, some other predator eats more urchins, and the otters could still be the main reason for the change.
choices.negation: Sea otters do not eat more sea urchins than every other predator in Calder Sound does.

choices.note: Tempting, since temperature could be a rival cause. But a temperature change need not have affected kelp. Negated (temperatures changed somewhat), the otters could still be the main reason. Not required.
choices.negation: Water temperatures in Calder Sound have changed at some point during the past twelve years.

choices.note: This is about what kelp does for otters, the reverse direction. Negated, nothing changes about why kelp expanded.
choices.negation: Expanded kelp forests do not provide sea otters with shelter from their own predators.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, urchins were too few to limit kelp before the otters came back. Then cutting urchin numbers can't explain the kelp boom, and the argument falls apart. Required.
choices.negation: Before the otters returned, sea urchins in Calder Sound were not numerous enough to limit the growth of its kelp forests.

choices.note: Too strong. Urchins just need to eat enough kelp to matter, not eat only kelp. Negated (they eat some other things too), the mechanism still works.
choices.negation: Sea urchins in Calder Sound eat some food other than kelp.

questions.stimulus: Public health director: Of the Fallon County residents who were treated for heat stroke last summer, 70 percent were over age 65. So residents of Fallon County who are over 65 are much more likely to suffer heat stroke than are younger residents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the public health director's reasoning?
choices: It presumes, without justification, that heat stroke is more dangerous for older residents than for younger ones.
It treats a factor that makes heat stroke more likely as though it were the only cause of heat stroke.
It fails to consider that some younger residents who suffered heat stroke may also have had other illnesses.
It confuses the claim that most heat stroke patients are over 65 with the claim that most residents over 65 suffer heat stroke.
It fails to consider what proportion of Fallon County's residents are over age 65.
questions.explanation: That 70 percent of patients were over 65 shows greater risk only if older people make up much less than 70 percent of the population; if most residents are over 65, the figure is unremarkable. E names this missing base rate. D is the tempting trap: it describes a real confusion, but the director never concludes that most older residents get heat stroke, only that they are more likely to than younger residents. Nothing in the argument concerns danger (A) or a sole cause (B).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fallon County residents over 65 are much more likely to suffer heat stroke than younger residents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70% of residents treated for heat stroke last summer were over 65.

breakdown.analysis: Missing base rate. 70% of patients being over 65 means more risk only if over-65s are a much smaller share of the population. Imagine a retirement county where 80% of residents are over 65: then 70% of patients being over 65 means they're actually less likely to get heat stroke. Lesson: a share of cases means nothing without the share of the population.

choices.note: The argument is about how likely heat stroke is, not how dangerous it is once you have it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: More older people go to the hospital for the flu, so the flu must be deadlier for them.

choices.note: The director never says age is the only cause. The conclusion is only about relative likelihood.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smoking raises lung cancer risk, so anyone with lung cancer must have smoked.

choices.note: Other illnesses among younger patients wouldn't change the comparison of rates. Off target.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Young people who got sick also had colds, so the heat wasn't really what made them sick.

choices.note: The trap. That confusion is a real flaw, but the director doesn't make it. The conclusion is "more likely than younger residents," not "most older residents get heat stroke."
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most car thieves are under 30, so most people under 30 steal cars.

choices.note: CORRECT. Whether 70% is alarming depends on what share of the county is over 65. Without that base rate, the figure can't show older residents are at higher risk.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: A court ruling deserves public confidence only if it is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow. But any ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists cannot be explained in such terms unless the court sets out the specialists' competing views in plain language. In the Marsh case, the appellate court's opinion did not set out in plain language the views of either side's forensic experts. So the court's ruling in the Marsh case does not deserve public confidence.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the legal scholar's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The appellate court's ruling in the Marsh case turned on a dispute between the two sides' forensic experts.
Any court ruling that sets out specialists' competing views in plain language is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow.
A court ruling that is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow deserves public confidence.
Most court rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists fail to set out the specialists' views in plain language.
The forensic experts in the Marsh case disagreed with each other about matters that ordinary citizens could not follow.
questions.explanation: The second rule applies only to rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists. If the Marsh ruling did (A), then because the experts' views were not set out plainly, the ruling was not explained in followable terms, and by the first rule it does not deserve confidence. E is the most attractive trap: it says the experts disagreed, but not that the ruling turned on their dispute, so the second rule still is not triggered. B and C reverse the stated conditionals, and D's 'most' says nothing about this case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Marsh ruling does not deserve public confidence.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Deserves confidence → explained in followable terms; ruling turns on specialist dispute → (followable only if specialists' views set out plainly); the Marsh opinion did not set out either side's forensic experts' views plainly.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: turns on specialist dispute AND views not set out plainly → not followable → doesn't deserve confidence. We know the views weren't set out plainly. What's missing is the trigger for rule 2: that the Marsh ruling actually turned on a dispute among specialists. Supply that and everything fires: specialist dispute + no plain explanation → not followable → no confidence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The ruling turned on the forensic experts' dispute. Since their views weren't set out plainly, the ruling wasn't explained in followable terms, and so it doesn't deserve confidence. Conclusion follows.
Reverses rule 2. Setting out views plainly → followable gives a way to be followable, not a way to fail. Doesn't help prove "no confidence."
Reverses rule 1. Followable → deserves confidence tells you what's enough for confidence, not what rules it out.
"Most" says nothing certain about Marsh. Also it never says Marsh turned on a specialist dispute.
The most attractive trap. The experts disagreed, but that doesn't mean the ruling turned on their disagreement. Rule 2 still isn't triggered.

questions.stimulus: Most commuters in Pell City choose between driving downtown and taking the train mainly on the basis of total travel time. The city plans to add express trains that would cut the train trip downtown by ten minutes. But the city also plans to close two of the three parking lots at the Maple Street station, where most train commuters board after driving there. Unless commuters can find parking quickly elsewhere, the time saved on the train may be lost searching for a space. So ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the city should cancel its plan to close the parking lots at the Maple Street station
adding express trains may not, by itself, make the train more attractive to commuters than it is now
the number of commuters who take the train will decline once the parking lots are closed
commuters care more about the availability of parking than about total travel time
most commuters who now drive downtown would switch to the train if parking at the station were expanded
questions.explanation: Commuters weigh total travel time, and the ten minutes saved on the train may be lost hunting for parking, so the express trains may fail to make the train more attractive; B matches the argument's cautious 'may.' C is the tempting trap but is too strong: the argument says only that the savings may be lost, not that ridership will fall. A draws a policy recommendation the argument does not reach, and D contradicts the first sentence.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Most Pell City commuters choose between driving and the train mainly on total travel time; 2) express trains would cut the train trip by ten minutes; 3) two of three parking lots at Maple Street station, where most train commuters park, will close; 4) unless commuters find parking quickly elsewhere, the time saved may be lost searching for a space.

breakdown.analysis: Commuters care about total time. Express trains save ten minutes, but parking hunts may eat those ten minutes. So the total trip may not get shorter, and the train may not become any more attractive. The key word is "may." The conclusion should be just as cautious: no predictions of decline, no policy orders.

choices.note: A policy recommendation the argument doesn't reach. It just warns that the savings may be lost; it never weighs whether to keep the lots.
CORRECT. The ten minutes saved may be lost to parking, and commuters judge by total time, so express trains alone may not make the train more attractive. Matches the argument's "may."
The tempting trap, but too strong. The argument says savings may be lost, not that ridership will fall. If parking is found quickly elsewhere, nothing changes.
Contradicts the first sentence: commuters choose mainly on total travel time. Parking matters only because it affects time.
A big prediction about switching that nothing supports. We don't know how many drivers would switch under any plan.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: The Halvorsen Museum should not lend its fragile, one-of-a-kind medieval tapestry to the touring exhibition, even though the tour would let many thousands of people see the tapestry who otherwise never would. Each move exposes the tapestry to a small but real risk of irreparable damage, and once it is damaged, no future visitor will ever see it as it is now.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the museum director's argument?
choices: A museum should lend its works only to exhibitions organized by institutions with expertise in conservation.
Museums should make the works in their collections accessible to as many people as possible.
A museum should not lend a work if the work could be damaged by conditions in the borrowing institution's galleries.
A museum should not subject an irreplaceable work to any risk of permanent damage solely in order to let more people see it.
The risk of damage to a work of art should be weighed against the educational benefit of showing it to new audiences.
questions.explanation: The director concedes the tour's benefit, wider viewing, but holds that a small risk of irreparable damage to a unique work outweighs it. D states that principle exactly, so the conclusion follows. E is the attractive trap: it describes weighing risk against benefit, but it does not say which way the balance comes out, so it cannot justify refusing the loan. C concerns the borrower's galleries, while the director's concern is the moves themselves, and B supports lending.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The museum should not lend its fragile, one-of-a-kind tapestry to the touring exhibition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The tour would let thousands more people see it (conceded); but each move carries a small, real risk of irreparable damage, and once damaged, no future visitor can see it as it is now.

breakdown.analysis: The director grants the benefit (more viewers) and still says no, because even a small risk of permanent damage to a one-of-a-kind work isn't worth it. The principle we need has to land on "don't lend": don't expose an irreplaceable work to any risk of permanent damage just to let more people see it. Lesson: a principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: About who organizes the exhibition, which the director never raises. The concern is the moves themselves. Doesn't justify refusing.
Supports lending. More access is the very thing the director is willing to give up.
About conditions in the borrower's galleries. The director's worry is the risk of each move, not the galleries.
CORRECT. Irreplaceable work, risk of permanent damage, purpose is letting more people see it: don't do it. Every piece matches the director's facts, and it comes out on the director's side.
The attractive trap. It says to weigh risk against benefit but doesn't say which wins. A principle that doesn't pick a side can't justify the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Most of the orchards in the Daltry region that were sprayed with kaolin clay last season suffered little sunburn damage to their fruit. Every orchard in the region that suffered little sunburn damage got a premium price for its apples. So some of the orchards in the region that were sprayed with kaolin clay got a premium price for their apples.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the musicians in the Fairview orchestra studied at a conservatory. Most musicians who studied at a conservatory can sight-read difficult scores. So some musicians in the Fairview orchestra can sight-read difficult scores.
Every bicycle sold at Corliss Cycles comes with a one-year warranty. Most bicycles with a one-year warranty are made overseas. So some bicycles sold at Corliss Cycles are made overseas.

Most of the restaurants that passed the city's health inspection last month had also been inspected the previous year. Every restaurant inspected the previous year was sent a reminder notice. So some restaurants that passed last month's inspection were sent a reminder notice.

Most of the novels on this year's prize shortlist were written by first-time authors. Some first-time authors have received writing grants. So some novels on the shortlist were written by authors who received writing grants.
Every greenhouse at the Ames nursery is heated by solar panels. No greenhouse heated by solar panels needs a backup generator. So no greenhouse at the Ames nursery needs a backup generator.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B is C, so some A are C. C has exactly this form (most restaurants that passed were inspected the year before; every one inspected then got a notice; so some that passed got a notice). A is the most tempting trap because it also concludes 'some,' but its second premise says 'most' rather than 'every,' and two 'most' statements need not overlap, so it is invalid. B and D are likewise invalid, and E is valid but has a different, all-and-none form.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some kaolin-sprayed orchards got a premium price for their apples.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most kaolin-sprayed orchards had little sunburn damage; every orchard with little sunburn damage got a premium price.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; every B is C; so some A are C. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: This one's valid. If most sprayed orchards had little damage, and all low-damage orchards got premium prices, then at least those sprayed, low-damage orchards got premium prices. So some sprayed orchards did. Look for the same "most... every... so some" shape. Watch for lookalikes where the second premise is only "most" or "some": those break the chain.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. Same "so some" ending, but the second premise is "most" about conservatory musicians in general, not "every." The orchestra's conservatory grads could all be in the minority who can't sight-read. Invalid.
Starts with "every," then "most" about bicycles in general. Corliss's bikes could all be in the warranty group made domestically. Invalid, and different order.

CORRECT. Most restaurants that passed were inspected the year before; every one inspected the year before got a notice; so some that passed got a notice. Most A are B, every B is C, some A are C. Exact match.
Second premise is "some," which can't connect. The shortlisted first-time authors might not be among those with grants. Invalid.
Valid, but a different form: every A is B, no B is C, so no A is C. All-and-none, not most-every-some.
